speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My point of privilege is based on citation 198 of Beauchesne's third edition:
Scandalous charges or imputations directed against members of a select committee are equivalent to libellous charges brought against the house itself.
In Saturday's issue of the Winnipeg Free Press there appears a story with respect to constituency changes in Manitoba. I read this sentence:
In drawing the redistribution map the Manitoba chairman said he and his fellow members had worked "on a scientific basis".
The chairman referred to is the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau). My point of privilege is that as one of the alleged fellow members of that committee I had nothing whatever to do with the drawing of the map. It was presented to the committee by the chairman. The same newspaper publishes two maps, one of the province as a whole, one of the city of Winnipeg, and says that they are the proposals of the provincial subcommittee.
As a member of that subcommittee I protest against this affront. They are only the proposals of the chairman himself.
Mr J. A. Ross (Souris): Mr. Speaker, on a matter of personal privilege, I wish also to refer to these constituency changes in Manitoba, without repeating what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said. He read the sentence which says that in drawing the redistribution map the Manitoba chairman said he and his fellow members had worked "on a scientific basis". I was a member of that subcommittee for Manitoba. The article also points out that this map is the proposal of the provincial subcommittee on federal redistribution. My matter of privilege is this. At our second subcommittee meeting we were handed a map by the chairman. There were only three of us present, the chairman, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself. We were told that this map was final and would be presented to the committee. I had nothing whatever to do with the drawing of this map, and I do not think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had either. We are not parties to the proposal which will be presented to the general committee, so that this article from that point of view is absolutely untrue.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several days ago, questions were asked about the recent meetings of the international wheat council held in London. The eighth session of the council, which was opened on April 17 to consider an extension of the international wheat agreement, adjourned on May 9.
At the conclusion of the meetings, a short statement was issued by the chairman of the council summarizing the proceedings which should, I think, be placed on the record. I quote:
The council has carried out a review of the provisions of the agreement and has decided that certain changes in the agreement would be desirable.

Wheat-International Agreement
On the major question of price, the council concluded that fuller examination was required of some of the factors affecting the maximum and minimum prices to be incorporated in an extended agreement. The council wished to examine further, among other things, whether at stated intervals there should be an automatic variation of maximum and minimum prices based on some index which would reflect changes in the general price level.
The council decided to set up a continuing committee to investigate this question of flexibility and other matters which require to be further explored beiore the council can reach conclusions upon them. This committee will report to the next regular bi-annual session of the council which will begin on the 1st July next.
Under a provision of the present agreement, the council is under obligation to communicate to the exporting and importing countries, not later than the 31st July, 1952, its recommendations regarding the extension of the agreement beyond the 31st July, 1953, when the present agreement expires. It will therefore be for the council during its regular session in July to make recommendations on this subject. These are expected to be of an interim character and the council's detailed recommendations on amendments to the agreement, including those on maximum and minimum prices, will be for decision when the council resumes its eighth session late in 1952.
That is the end of the official statement by the council. May I add a word or two about the attitude taken by Canada at the meetings:
The Canadian delegation went to London prepared to negotiate a renewal of the agreement. For that purpose, the government appointed five advisers from the principal producer organizations in the prairie provinces to be available for consultations on the spot.
With the unanimous agreement of all the advisers, the Canadian delegation took the position that a substantial increase in prices was justified in a renewed agreement and made proposals along that line. The United States and Australia, the two other principal exporters, also put forward proposals for a substantially higher range of prices.
It soon appeared that there was a wide gap between the respective views of the exporting countries, on the one hand, and those of the importing countries, on the other hand, as to the level of the price range for a renewed agreement. This disparity in views was not altogether surprising considering that a renewed agreement would not come into effect until August, 1953, some fifteen months hence.
At the meeting just concluded, no country-indicated that it was not prepared to continue the agreement. It was agreed, as the official statement indicates, that full-scale negotiations should be resumed at a later date, towards the end of the present calendar year, when all parties will have a clearer impression of the conditions which will prevail at the time that a renewed agreement would come into operation.
May I say in conclusion that the government is particularly grateful for the assistance


given by the advisers from the farm organizations who, I am glad to say, gave complete support at all times to the views and proposals put forward by the Canadian delegation at the conference.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN TROOPS AT KOJE ISLAND PRISONER-OF-WAR CAMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement in regard to reports that Canadian troops have been moved to Koje island, in Korea, to participate in the guarding of communist prisoners of war on that island.
On the afternoon of Thursday, May 22, the chief of the general staff received a telegram from the officer commanding, 25th Canadian infantry brigade, Korea, to the effect that he had received an order from the first (commonwealth) division issued in accordance with a request from the United Nations command to post a company from the brigade to guard duty at the prisoner-of-war camp on Koje island, and that he was accordingly assigning a company from the Royal Canadian Regiment for this duty.
On receipt of this message an inquiry regarding the order was immediately made in Washington. The inquiry confirmed that the order had been given, and that orders had also been given for the posting of units from certain other national forces under the United Nations command to similar duty. It also appeared that the movement of the Canadian troops in question was under way.
The government feels that it is essential that the Canadian policy in respect of the breaking up of the Canadian brigade for miscellaneous duties in Korea should be made clear. A note has accordingly been presented to the state department in Washington.
The following is the text of this note:
The Canadian government recognizes the importance of re-establishing and maintaining effective control over communist prisoners of war captured in Korean operations. The Canadian government also recognizes that custody of prisoners of war is a military responsibility which should be performed in accordance with military requirements.
It has, however, been a long established policy of the Canadian government that Canadian forces dispatched abroad for military operations should remain under Canadian command and control and that, except in the event of a military emergency which does not permit of time for consultation, no part of these forces should be detached therefrom except after consultation and with the agreement of the Canadian government.
The Canadian government therefore views with concern the dispatch of a company of the 25th infantry brigade to Koje island without prior consultation with the Canadian government, and hopes that it may be possible to re-unite this

company with the rest of the Canadian brigade as soon as possible. Meanwhile, the Canadian forces concerned will, of course, carry out loyally the orders of the unified command with respect to participation in guarding prisoners of war on Koje island. The Canadian government also wishes to be reassured that, if it is proposed in the future to detach any Canadian forces from Canadian command and control for military or other duties, this will be done only after consultation and with the consent of the Canadian government, except in the event of a military emergency which does not permit of time for such consultation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN TROOPS AT KOJE ISLAND PRISONER-OF-WAR CAMP
speechtext: May I ask a question arising out of the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs? In view of the part Canadians are playing in connection with the custody of prisoners of war, whether for a temporary or a prolonged period, will Canada have a voice in other matters with reference to prisoners of war, particularly in relation to the truce talks?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN TROOPS AT KOJE ISLAND PRISONER-OF-WAR CAMP
speechtext: I do not wish at this time to add anything to the note I have just read. However, in regard to consultation, I should point out that there are regular meetings in Washington in which Canadian representatives, as well as the representatives of other countries with forces in Korea, participate. In those meetings we are kept generally informed as to the progress or lack of progress of the truce and other negotiations in Korea; and included in those negotiations of course is the question of prisoners of war.

speechtext: How were the arms, stores and equipment which were sent from Canada to NATO checked and accounted for on arrival in Europe?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Canadian army personnel in conjunction with the shipping agents check by means of ordnance issue vouchers all equipment and stores as they are loaded on the vessel.
Ocean bills of lading are prepared by the shipping agent of company concerned.
One copy each of the ordnance issue vouchers and the ocean bills of lading are retained by the captain of the ship.
One copy of the ordnance issue vouchers and the ocean bills of lading are forwarded to the official representative of the recipient country.
One copy of the ocean bills of lading is retained by army headquarters as a receipt for the equipment and stores shipped.
The recipient country is financially responsible for the movement of the equipment and stores overseas and therefore responsible for its checking and accounting on arrival in Europe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE OF SECTIONS ONE TO THREE UNTIL MAY 30, 1953
speechtext:
the following resolution:
That, whereas section four of the Emergency Powers Act, being chapter five of the statutes of 1951 (first session), provides that sections one to three of that act expire on the thirty-first day of May, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-two, provided that if at any time while they are in force addresses are presented to the governor general by the Senate and House of Commons, respectively, praying that they should be continued in force for a further period, not exceeding one year from the time at which they would otherwise expire, and the governor in council so orders, they shall continue in force for that further period.
And whereas it is desirable to continue the said sections in force up to and including the thirtieth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three.
The following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency the Right Honourable Vincent Massey, Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour, Governor General, and Commander-inChief of Canada:
May it please Your Excellency:
We, Her Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, respectfully approach Your Excellency praying that sections one to three of the Emergency Powers Act be continued in force up to and including the thirtieth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to have parliament consider whether or not the special responsibility put upon the government to deal with possible emergencies which might arise because of the threatening world situation should be continued beyond the initial period provided for in the Emergency Powers Act, being chapter 5 of the statutes of 1951. The
Emergency Powers Act preamble of chapter 5 of the statutes of 1951 contains the following recitals:
Whereas an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada;
And whereas it is essential that emergency powers be conferred to enable measures to be taken as urgently required from time to time to carry out adequate defence preparations, to regulate the economy of Canada to meet the needs of defence and to stabilize the economy and to safeguard it from disruption that may result from defence preparation in Canada or from emergency measures taken in other countries, in order that defence preparations may not be impeded;
And whereas it is preferable that the necessary emergency powers be exercised under special authority from parliament rather than that the War Measures Act be brought into force so long as present efforts to avert war are continuing and, moreover, it is not desirable that the wide powers conferred by that act to interfere with the fundamental liberties of the individual should now be brought into operation:
Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
The powers which it was made the responsibility of the government to exercise if and when necessary were expressed in section 2, subsections 1 and 2, which I think we should have on the record at this time. Section 2, subsection 1, is in the following terms:
2. (I) The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existing international emergency deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the governor in council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, that is to say:
(a)	control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs;
(b)	control of communications and means of communication;
(c)	control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada; and the movements of vessels;
(d)	transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;
(e)	trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture; and
(f)	imposition and recovery, in connection with any scheme of control, of fees or charges payable to the Receiver General of Canada or into any fund or account established by order or regulation for the purposes of the scheme of control.
Subsection 2 qualified these powers in the following way:
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained therein, the powers conferred on the governor in council by subsection one do not include power to make orders or regulations in relation to
(a)	arrest, except as incidental to proceedings under section three; detention, exclusion or deportation of any person;
(b)	censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings; or
(c)	expenditure of moneys otherwise than in accordance with an appropriation by parliament except expenditure of moneys from any fund or

Emergency Powers Act
account established by order or regulation in connection with a scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control.
Subsection 4 of the same section provided that any order or regulation made under the act would be tabled within five days from the date thereof if parliament was then in session, or within five days from the opening of parliament if it were not in session at the time. Subsection 5 provided that any order might be annulled by resolution of the Senate and the House of Commons within forty days from the tabling thereof. It will be remembered that an undertaking was given by the government that if there was any desire to propose such a motion an opportunity would be provided for its being dealt with expeditiously. Section 4 of the act provided that it would expire on the 31st of May but might be extended for a further period of not more than twelve months on resolution of the two houses of parliament. The resolution you have just read, Mr. Speaker, provides parliament with an opportunity to determine whether or not it should be so extended.
When the act was passed I think most members will recall that some were inclined to look upon it as a provision whereby the government was taking from parliament the right to exercise powers which normally belonged to parliament. In reality the purpose was to increase the responsibility of the government, subject to the control of parliament, to meet such emergencies as it might suddenly become necessary to deal with in order to preserve the peace, order and good government of the country in the then threatening international situation. It was not that the government wanted greater powers. It was passed because it was deemed to be a wise precaution to make it the responsibility of the government to act quickly if and when prompt action might be necessary, and to be able to take such action without proclaiming the more sweeping War Measures Act unless it became absolutely necessary to put that act into operation.
Fortunately for the people of Canada as well as for the government, since the Emergency Powers Act came into force it has not been necessary to have recourse to its provisions very often. In all, nineteen orders have been made under it. Five of these orders have to do with the great lakes seamen's security regulations. They are P.C. 1439 of March 22, 1951, P.C. 2101 of April 26, 1951, P.C. 2847 of June 4, 1951, P.C. 3855 of July 24, 1951, and P.C. 2306 of May 2, 1952. All these orders of course have the same aim and purpose. The reason why there have been five is that modifications have been made from time to time as experience showed that the existing order might

cause some inconveniences in the trade which were not really necessary from the point of view of the security purposes envisaged by the regulations.
The Department of Labour and the Department of Transport have been in constant touch with ship owners operating on the great lakes and with the labour unions representing the men working the ships. These interested parties have from time to time recommended modifications. These have been considered by our security officials, and in many instances it has been felt that the representations could be recommended for modifications without imperilling the purpose for which the regulations were made.
As to the other fourteen orders, three have to do with the establishment of priorities control and the appointment of controllers. The orders are P.C. 2399 of May 16, 1951, P.C. 2621 of May 24, 1951, and P.C. 5645 of October 22, 1951. The first one created the order with respect to controls. The other two had to do with the appointment of officials to exercise the powers directed to be exercised by the regulations.
Then there were two orders, P.C. 4535 and P.C. 4558 of August 29, 1951, having to do with transport control and the appointment of a transport controller. It will be remembered that was done to facilitate the distribution of the required freight cars throughout the prairie provinces in order to move more expeditiously the grain that was destined for export.
There was also P.C. 1234 of March 3, 1952, made to control the export and import of cattle and meat products to and from the United States consequent upon the embargo resulting from United States laws when it was ascertained that foot-and-mouth disease had broken out in Canada. This order could probably have been made solely under the Export and Import Permits Act, but reference was made as well to the Emergency Powers Act so as to make it perfectly sure that the validity of the order could not be successfully challenged.
Then there was a security order, P.C. 3486 of July 4, 1951, which was exempted from publication for the reasons which I explained in the house on October 24 last in answer to a question from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowlesh Interested members may find this explanation with respect to that order in Hansard on page 342.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Is that the only one that was exempted from publication?

speechtext:
That is the only one that was exempted from publication. I had a

word with the leaders of the various groups in the house in order to explain the general purpose of the order and the reasons why it was desirable that it should not be published. There was one other order made, P.C. 3484, of August 8, 1951, concerning the operation by agencies of the United States government and the United States defence forces of radio stations in Canada in connection with our joint arrangements for effective protection of the North American continent.
Another one of very small importance but which it was found very convenient to be able to make was P.C. 6598 of December 6, 1951, exempting from customs duties personal gifts of a value not exceeding $25 from members of the Canadian forces serving abroad and addressed to relatives or friends in Canada.
Those orders are still in force, and with the exception of the one dealing with the exportation and importation of livestock and meats, depend for their validity upon the Emergency Powers Act. That one might probably be sustained under the provisions of the Export and Import Permits Act.
There were five other orders which were passed under the Emergency Powers Act to put into effect at once provisions that it was intended to have enacted in a permanent form by legislation at the first convenient opportunity. They are as follows: P.C. 2932 of June 7, 1951, extending the provisions of the Defence Services Pension Act to members of the regular forces granted temporary commissions; and P.C. 3417 of July 4, 1951, concerning the disposition of offences committed prior to the coming into force of the code of service discipline. Both these orders have since been replaced by legislation included in the statute adopted under the title of the Canadian Forces Act, 1951. On July 31, 1951, there was an order made, P.C. 3415, concerning the agricultural products board which has since been established in legislative form by the Agricultural Products Board Act. On April 4, 1951, there was an order made, P.C. 1608, which it was hoped to replace by legislation before this time. It was to substitute other metals for nickel, because of the scarcity of nickel, in the Canadian five-cent piece. That is being covered by a proposal included in a bill to be introduced at this session concerning the currency and exchange fund acts.
On September 26, 1951, P.C. 5122 was made operative postponing the weigh-over of grain required by the Canada Grain Act. That was intended to be covered by legislation and there is a section to that effect in the Canada Grain Act amendment now before parliament.
Emergency Powers Act
Those are the nineteen orders that were made under these emergency powers. Hon. members will recognize the fact that no one of them has been challenged as improper by any member of parliament; and I think this list shows how fortunate we have been during that period in not having to deal with any more serious or troublesome emergencies than those to which the orders refer. It also shows how careful the government has been not to exercise the power to do anything not urgently required for the peace, order and good government of the country.
That has been a fortunate situation since the statute came into force, but the factual international situation set out in the preamble to this statute is much the same today as it was when that statute was adopted. When we are appropriating billions of dollars to meet the dangers of that international situation, we are doing it not because we expect to have our forces engaged in actual warfare but as a deterrent and so that they might be ready should the deterring purpose not be realized. We have thought that, while we are doing that, it is desirable that there be ready for use, if required, some extraordinary powers, though we sincerely hope that they may not have to be used. However, that is a matter for the houses of parliament to decide. It means placing continuing additional responsibility on the government.
I feel it is the government's duty to recommend to parliament that the provisions of this act be continued in existence for a further period of twelve months, giving all the same undertakings that were given when it was originally enacted as to making opportunity for bringing to a decision any resolution or vote designed to set aside any regulation that might be made. Under the present international situation I think it would be taking undesirably some risk in not having an instrument capable of being used expeditiously if conditions developed that required it to be used.
I trust that the experience of the last fourteen months-it is fourteen months now since the act was passed-will satisfy the uneasiness any hon. member might have felt at the possible danger of its being in the power of the government to discharge responsibility to meet an emergent situation rapidly. I can assure hon. members that there is no desire by the government to have extraordinary powers; but we feel that we would not be fulfilling our duties if, as the government, we did not recommend to parliament the desirability of having those extraordinary powers in reserve at a time when we still feel that the international situation requires the appropriating of these large sums of money to build

Emergency Powers Act up defence forces to meet what might arise, although we sincerely hope-and I think with some confidence after these many months- that it will not arise. I therefore recommend for the serious consideration of hon. members the question as to whether or not these powers should remain available for another period of twelve months.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE OF SECTIONS ONE TO THREE UNTIL MAY 30, 1953
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in support of the motion the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has laid before the house the general provisions of the act itself and has indicated his own belief that the wording of the motion is one which should be accepted by hon. members of this house. The words of the motion which really raise a question for the consideration of all hon. members are as follows:
... it is desirable to continue the said sections in force up to and including the thirtieth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three.
The question before this house, Mr. Speaker, is whether it is appropriate for the representatives of the people, who were sent here to do the business of the people, to delegate their authority to the government, no matter what assurances the government may give as to its intentions to employ the terms of that act. This is not something that can be disposed of simply by a statement that the act has been in force for a year, and that it has only been used on eighteen occasions to pass laws by way of order in council. I submit that what should be considered by hon. members on both sides of the house is what the effect of this act is, and whether under any conditions which now exist the members are justified in delegating to the executive practically all of their responsibilities, subject only to the restraint that the government may exercise in employing the powers given by such an act.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said in effect, and I do not quote his exact words, that the purpose of this resolution is to determine whether the government should have the emergency powers to deal with situations which might arise in this uncertain world in which we are now living. I believe the question which should be determined by the members is a much more fundamental question than that. The Prime Minister has said that the government has no desire to possess extraordinary powers. He has given the assurance that it is not the intention of the government to employ these powers in any manner that would derogate from the authority of parliament. He has pointed out also that there are provisions for the tabling of orders in council, and that assurance has been given that if it were


desired to present a substantive motion for the purpose of having the house consider any order in council the government would be ready to expedite the hearing of that motion.
I am not questioning the desire of the Prime Minister to interpret what might be in his mind in regard to the employment of an act of this kind. I can only repeat that it is the duty of every one of us to examine this act and say to ourselves, is the power conferred by this act a power which should be conferred upon any government in a time of general peace? Is this an act which should be passed by a parliament which is still able to maintain ordinary contact with those people whom it represents? Is this an act that should be passed at a time when there is no dislocation in our communications, and no threat of any dislocation in our communications? Is it an act which should be passed at a time when we realize that no matter what grave threats may impend, and no matter how very real the struggle may be for those who are now engaged in Korea, the life of our people is one which has the general appearance of peace? Those are the questions which should be in our minds. It is no answer to say, as some hon. members are inclined to say, that they have complete confidence in the government.
The question is whether this is an act which should be passed, no matter what government may be in power. It is that test which should be applied to any legislation which receives the approval of this house. The Prime Minister has spoken of the fact that the government has been careful not to employ the powers of this act too frequently or too extensively. I would point out that a number of the powers which have been exercised are powers which could have been exercised quite conveniently in another way. It seems to me that the very fact that some of those things have been done demonstrates how readily any government falls into the habit of a more convenient procedure which does not call for debate in the House of Commons.
As has been explained, several of the orders in council relate to the great lakes seamen's security regulations. As I understand it, the effect of these regulations was largely designed to provide a method by which communist activities amongst great lakes seamen might be dealt with. They were designed to provide a method for screening those who might have communist sympathies. At this point no one in the house will forget the number of occasions upon which I have sought amendments to the Criminal Code, so that in the form of clear and definitive law there might be a provision which would make it possible to deal with communists here in

Canada. I do not believe that communist activities, which are designed and intended to undermine the strength of the state at a time when we are spending so much money and putting forward so much human effort to prevent communist aggression, should be permitted in this country. I have made it clear on every occasion that I have raised this subject that I do not think there should be arbitrary action in regard to communists. I believe in the rule of law. I believe we should define the offence. Unless the government is able to define the offence, then it should not be passing orders in council which relate to that offence which they say they cannot define, if there is some offence which can be described as communist activity or a specific activity of that nature, then it is either definable or it is not. If it is definable, the offence should be clearly stated in the Criminal Code. If it is not definable, then it should not be the subject of arbitrary provisions adopted behind closed doors.
I find that there was an order in council passed to deal with the five-cent piece. This was not a case where the famous quotation could be used, "not a five-cent piece". This was one case where the five-cent piece was regarded as being of sufficient importance for the government to deal with it, and thev dealt with it by this order in council under the act because it was convenient to deal with it in that way. The question arises as to why this was not dealt with by an amendment to the Currency Act. The date indicates the reason this government conveniently dealt with it in that way. That order was passed on April 4, 1951. The house was sitting at that time. An amendment to the Currency Act could very conveniently have been introduced in this house and the members of parliament could have dealt with it in the ordinary way.
Then also there was an order passed on March 3, dealing with the importation of cattle and animal feed into Canada from the United States. True, it may have been convenient to pass this by order in council, but again may I point out that the house was sitting. Just a few days before we had been asked to deal expeditiously with a measure which was related to this subject. It was an act to provide compensation for those whose animals were destroyed as a result of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. The house by unanimous consent set aside other business and proceeded to deal with this measure. It would have been quite as easy to have dealt with that measure in the house. If it had been dealt with, it probably would have been suggested that this subject be given more consideration than was given to it at the time. It might have been suggested that the use of
Emergency Powers Act this measure, which looked a little like retaliation, was not exactly the way to gain the good will of our friends in the United States at a time when we had every reason to seek their good will to solve some of our unfortunate difficulties.
As one goes through these orders in council one finds that most of them do deal with matters that could very much better have been dealt with by amendments to existing legislation. In fact, it would seem that every one of them, except the one which provided for secrecy, in regard to certain orders in council, could best have been passed in that way. When I say except that order I do not mean that that order could not have been placed before the house. I think that is the very kind of order that should have called for an act of this parliament. If any order in council is not going to be published, is not going to be communicated to the members of parliament or to the public, then most assuredly the circumstances under which that power is to be exercised by the government should be stated in the clearest terms, and only in the most express wording should this parliament confer such extraordinary powers upon this or any other government.
Having dealt with the kind of orders in council that were passed, may I point out that when the Prime Minister speaks of the protection that is available by virtue of the fact that the orders in council, except those cloaked with secrecy, and the special order I have mentioned, should be tabled in this house, and that the government would entertain a motion to discharge any of those orders if such a motion were presented, the possibility of such a motion offers very little real opportunity to deal with this question. I can think of very few cases where the government would not immediately say: This is a challenge to the government; this must be dealt with as a want of confidence motion. And it would be a want of confidence motion; it would be a motion which declared that the house did not have confidence that the government had properly exercised its authority. The history of the voting of hon. members during the life of the present parliament is not such as to suggest that, from the practical as opposed to the theoretical point of view, the opportunities provided by the possibility of such a motion have any real value to hon. members.
True, we learn about these orders in council in due course. True, the orders in council, except the one providing for secrecy, do not appear to have dealt with subjects of major importance, unless perhaps in so far as the order in council in regard to the importation of animals and feed products from the United

Emergency Powers Act States may be regarded as important. But I think we should examine the attitude of this government in regard to orders in council generally before dismissing too lightly the possibility that anything might occur in regard to which there would not be general approval in this house.
Even if under this act up to this point there may not be substantial grounds for objection, I would like to point out the attitude of this government in regard to the exercise of some of its powers by order in council. It will be recalled by all hon. members that at the time the question was raised about the possibility of General Kurt Meyer's release during the session of this house last fall, the government dismissed in rather peremptory manner any suggestion that there might be concern that General Kurt Meyer, who had been whisked so surprisingly away from Canada back to his homeland, might in fact be released at any time by the Canadian government without this house knowing about it.
Now, while this was done under another act, I must confess that I for one found a great deal more importance attached to the fact that the order in council had been passed which released Wilhelm Ossenbach than I did to the actual fact that this man had been released, because at the very time that we were raising the question about the possibility of Kurt Meyer's being released, another German prisoner, who had been sentenced to fifteen years in prison in connection with the shooting of a Canadian prisoner of war, had been released by order in council as of October 3 last. That order in council was not tabled until November. By that time Wilhelm Ossenbach had been at large for more than a month. There may have been reasons why this was done, but the question does arise as to exactly what the difference in principle would be in the case of Wilhelm Ossenbach and in the case of Kurt Meyer, except that Kurt Meyer had been brought over to Canada. The only reason that Kurt Meyer happened to be brought to Canada was that he had been found guilty and sentenced to death. It was because of the commutation of the sentence that he was brought back to Canada under rather unusual circumstances. Then, as hon. members will recall, he left Canada under equally unusual circumstances, and the next we heard of him was that he was in the bosom of his family back in Germany. By the time that hon. members knew anything about it, it was so much a matter that had already been done that the possibility of undoing it was indeed very remote.

Then again, to refer to something that hon. members seem to think has been mentioned so often that we do not want to hear about it again, may I refer to something that does need to be cleared up, and that has not yet been cleared up, but which again illustrates the manner in which the government does employ its powers by order in council. I refer to the fact that this government by order in council, under an act other than the one now before us, saw fit to permit communists to man and operate ships, and to continue to man and operate ships, under the Canadian flag. The company to which that privilege was granted was a Canadian company incorporated for the one purpose of giving Canadian identity to those who hold nominal ownership of the ships built in Canada for the Ming Sung company. That Canadian corporate ownership was provided because the head office of the company was in communist China, where it still operates.
It has been said that it was not desirable to withdraw the right to Canadian registry of these ships under the control of a communist company operating in waters where they might well be carrying contraband that would be used against Canadian armed men. The explanation given was that an attempt was being made to recover the money which had been advanced very generously by the Canadian government to make these ships available for the Ming Sung company. So far as we know, those ships, now entirely under communist control, are still flying the Canadian flag. So far as we have been informed, this government has not yet seen fit to restore the dignity of the Canadian flag in those waters by taking the very simple steps available to it of repudiating and rescinding this most unusual favour accorded to a company operating in that area.
I mention these orders in council because what happened in those two cases-and a number of other illustrations could be given to show what has occurred in other respects- do not suggest that the House of Commons should be too ready or too willing to extend blanket powers to this government on the basis of its actual record in dealing with public business by orders in council in some other cases.
I hope hon. members will consider this matter from the point of view of the atmosphere in which the measure was presented originally and the atmosphere in which we are considering the resolution now before the house. At the time the measure was originally presented conditions were very different from what they are today. As I recall it, the United Nations forces had just liberated Seoul

after a very threatening communist sweep, through Korea. Enemy resistance along the 38th parallel was building up. There was every reason to believe that a great offensive against our forces was under way. The whole atmosphere was entirely different from what it is today.
At that time we did oppose the adoption of these wide and unrestrained powers. At that time we did point out the danger of dealing with the subject in this way rather than by giving specific powers in certain specific fields. We did raise those objections, however, remembering what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) had said at that time when setting out the reasons why it was important to have such a measure adopted. On February 1 last year, as reported at page 29 of Hansard, the Prime Minister indicated that a bill of this kind would be introduced. These are his words as they appear in Hansard of that date:
We will seek, by the legislation forecast in the speech from the throne, to secure powers additional to those the governor in council already has. By proclaiming the War Measures Act on the ground of apprehended war we could have all those powers, but we prefer to leave it to parliament to say whether there is a sufficient emergency to justify a departure from regular constitutional procedure and the regular constitutional distribution of powers between the federal and provincial authorities.
The Prime Minister clearly indicated something about which I have expressed concern on a number of occasions. He expressed concern about departure from regular constitutional procedure and the regular constitutional distribution of powers between federal and provincial authorities. From the Prime Minister's own words there can be no doubt whatever that the measure now before us does depart from the normal constitutional distribution of power between the federal and provincial authorities, and that it does constitute a departure from regular constitutional procedure.
In saying that, there is of course the -reservation that it constitutes a departure *only to the extent that the government may *exercise the powers conferred upon it. Nevertheless, in the words of the Prime Minister himself, it is perfectly clear that this measure does give to the government powers to disregard the constitutional division of responsibility and authority between federal and provincial governments as laid down originally in the British North America Act.
There were other reasons given for the -introduction of the measure. As reported at
Emergency Powers Act page 185 of Hansard for February 8, 1951, the Minister of Defence Production said this:
In closing, I would like to say a few words about price control. The speech from the throne indicates the intention of the government to introduce a bill which will, if approved, confer upon the executive powers to impose price controls and other related controls for the purpose of maintaining economic stability.
These broad powers are being introduced to the end that the government will be in a position to take whatever action appears to be necessary from time to time.
Introduction of this legislation does not mean that the present intention is to impose over-all price and wage controls, although there is always the possibility that events will develop in such a way that general price and wage ceilings are appropriate and workable.
While it is true that the Minister of Defence Production indicated that it was not then the intention to introduce price controls, he clearly stated that one of the purposes of the introduction of this measure was so that they might be in a position to take such further steps by way of controls as would become necessary under the emergency.
Since that time events have taken a course which rightly or wrongly the government has interpreted as justifying the removal of certain controls which they did introduce. As an example, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced that the credit restrictions were being removed it was with the assurance that there had been such a return to normal conditions that he was justified in following that course. Moreover, at the time that other restrictions were removed the same explanation was given. The whole attitude of this government has been that in recent months there has been an improvement in the situation which makes it possible to relax controls. That being so, there certainly is not the pressure for the almost unrestrained powers that there was at that time.
I would place before members of this house principles which it seems to me are challenged by this legislation to an extent that did not seem necessary elsewhere under the very uncertain conditions then existing. I wish to emphasize the dangers that are inherent in legislation of this nature, dangers which have been examined by the most competent constitutional authorities and which have also been indicated by responsible writers in the press of this country as well as certain members of parliament on both sides of the house.
Most hon. members have read a book written some years ago which I think bears careful rereading today. I refer to "The New Despotism" by the late Lord Hewart of Bury. In that famous book he examined the danger of legislation by order in council as distinguished from laws passed by the

Emergency Powers Act representatives of the people. He pointed out that with the change that had taken place over the years certain administrative laws had become necessary to deal with the fast-moving and increasingly complex society in which we now live. He then made this further significant comment, and I quote from page 21 of that book:
"With us," as Professor Dicey says, "every official, from the Prime Minister down to a constable or a collector of taxes, is under the same responsibility for every act done without legal justification as any other citizen. The reports abound with cases in which officials have been brought before the courts, and made, in their personal capacity, liable to punishment, or to the payment of damages, for acts done in their official character but in excess of their lawful authority. A colonial governor, a secretary of state, a military officer, and all subordinates, though carrying out the commands of their official superiors, are as responsible for any act which the law does not authorize as is any private and unofficial person."
It may well be said by someone who is mentally at this moment justifying the introduction of this, "But are you aware that this act is an act which was passed by parliament and that what Lord Hewart was referring to at that point was the responsibility of everyone from the Prime Minister down to be answerable under the law?" My point is that the protection of the citizen described by Lord Hewart in those words is denied by the adoption of laws of this kind. It is only when clearly stated laws exist that the citizen has any protection against the Prime Minister or officials or others who may do things that may be contrary to his best interests. If we believe in the rule of law as opposed to the rule of dictate then we must be concerned with any measure which removes from the citizen those rights against anyone in authority which were so clearly described by Lord Hewart as being the very foundation of our free democracy.
I go on to further quotations from Lord Hewart where he deals with the dangers of legislation of this kind. He pointed out in his book that in Great Britain there had been those who justified the extension of administrative law by comparing the administrative law in Great Britain with the droit admini-stratif of France. But Lord Hewart went on to point out that the administrative law of France was something entirely different. He pointed out that under the different system which accepted that kind of law as a matter of tradition, nevertheless they had placed safeguards over the employment of laws of that kind which were not provided in Great Britain or any other corresponding parliamentary jurisdiction where administrative law was adopted.
He pointed out that the administrative law of France was placed under a tribunal of

the highest standing which reviewed those laws from time to time impartially and without any relation to the political complexion of those who had passed the law. Then he went on to say that in so far as these laws were concerned it was not enough to find out who were the individuals who were passing the law and then feel some measure of confidence that the men then responsible would not abuse them. He pointed out that laws that are passed should be regarded from the impersonal point of view. They should be examined as laws that might be administered by any government, and at no time should anyone seek to hide the dangers of administrative law by virtue of the fact that the men then exercising that power might be men who commanded general confidence.
The interesting thing, however, is that when Lord Hewart wrote about this subject some years ago he was merely dealing with administrative laws passed under acts which most clearly set out the subject matter that would be dealt with by the government. Having regard to the strength of his language in condemning administrative laws which supplant the rights of parliament, one can only guess that even Lord Hewart of Bury, with a tradition of carefully chosen words, would have written in a most explosive manner about an act which places practically all powers in the hands of the government subject only to their own idea as to the reservations that they might make upon the exercise of their powers.
Nor has it been only at Westminster that those charged with responsibility have warned of these dangers. In this house the present member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has discussed this matter on different occasions. I find that he discussed it on one occasion on March 21, 1946, as found at page 169 of Hansard. The hon. member for Quebec South, who I believe is the dean of the House of Commons, and who has demonstrated a deep and profound knowledge of the constitutional background of our proceedings, was dealing with this very subject of administrative law and emergency powers which confer sweeping authority of that kind. He pointed out that in his opinion neither the then prime minister nor the then minister of justice would in himself be likely to seriously abuse powers that might be conferred in that way. Since the hon. member for Quebec Soutk h*s so often spoken on behalf of what he believes to be the real principles of the Liberal party, may I recall what he said on that occasion after stating very clearly that he did not think that the prime minister of that time or the minister of justice of that time, who is now the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), would

himself contemplate any abuses. In spite of that statement of his own conviction this is what he said, as found at page 171 of Hansard:
But may I point out that neither of these men has any guarantee of immortality. Neither is there any guarantee in our political life that the political wheel of fortune may not some day turn. And the numbers brought up on that political wheel of fortune may not always be the numbers of men in whom this country has the same faith and confidence as it has in the men who are now at the helm of affairs.
Then he went on to outline the dangers inherent in legislation of this kind, dangers that could not be dismissed by expressing confidence in the individuals who would be charged with the responsibility of administering legislation of this nature that might be adopted. Then he used these words, to be found at page 172 of Hansard for March 21, 1946:
We have fought a victorious war after four years. We have talked glibly of the new order which was to follow it, and it almost appears to me as though we the victors had taken on the manners and customs of the vanquished.
These words were not spoken by any member on this side of the house. They were spoken by one who had been a member of the government during the years of the war. He was referring only to the employment of similar powers, but at a time when stronger arguments for the employment of such powers could have been put forward he said that it almost seemed to him as though we the victors were taking on the manners and the customs of the vanquished. Moreover, the same member for Quebec South had this to say in an article published in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 22, 1948:
When it is made clear that special extraordinary powers are absolutely necessary in order to deal with certain contingencies, let parliament delegate these powers, but only to the minister who shall be specifically mentioned in the legislation, and who shall be answerable to parliament for the exercise thereof. Moreover, the special authority conferred should be for specific purposes and the objects clearly stated in the legislation. The authority itself should be limited in extent to that which is required for the specific purposes-no omnibus clauses with a little more for good measure "in ease they were needed." Finally, this authority granted to the minister should be limited as to time and the law itself reenacted at each session of parliament if the contingency continues to exist.
May I point out that this hon. member, who was a member of the government and served in a very responsible post during the war years, touches two vital points with regard to the adoption of any legislation of this kind now or on any other occasion. First, it should only confer powers upon a specific minister in relation to a specific subject. Second, that power should be clearly defined, the objects for which the legislation is presented should be clearly stated, and the circumstances under which the minister can
Emergency Powers Act employ such power with the support of the government should be described in the clearest and most limited terms.
I submit that the hon. member for Quebec South has stated a proposition that should receive the support of every hon. member in the house. Nor has the argument been confined to members in the house. I want to quote some of the things that have been said by others outside the house because I regard the principle now under consideration as one of fundamental importance, and one which perhaps did not receive as complete and vigorous attention as it deserved last year. Actually, in the hands of those who were prepared to abuse such power, this bill could mean the end of parliament itself, nothing less. It could provide someone with the opportunity to repeat the famous speech of Cromwell when he wound up the parliament of Britain. There is no use saying that no hon. member in the house would think of doing that.
Hon. members of this house have seen some strange things done. They have seen some remarkable examples of government reluctance to produce information, and they have seen some rather remarkable orders in council passed under other legislation. But whether or not there were a single example that should put this house on guard when they are asked to extend this power at this time, may I remind the members of this house that not only have we the arguments and the advice of a man like Lord Hewart of Bury, not only have we the advice of a man Who has served as a member of this House of Commons and who has the longest experience in parliamentary procedure of any member now in this house, but we also have the expression of opinion of responsible individuals and members of the press outside.
At a time when this matter was under consideration last year Toronto Saturday Night, for instance, had this to say in regard to this very act which was passed then at a time when there was a much greater atmosphere of emergency and urgency than is apparent in any action of the government at this time. I quote from what appeared on March 20, 1951 in Saturday Night:
It is good that Canadians should wish their government to have all the powers it needs to ensure our making a fair contribution to the western alliance. But it is disquieting that the public should appear so little concerned about the ultimate right of parliament to have knowledge of, to enquire into, to criticize, and if necessary, to overrule any use that the government may make of these extraordinary powers.
Then after further discussion of this measure in an objective manner the Toronto Saturday Night has this to say:
Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Garson and the ether legal talent on the government side have shown an

Emergency Powers Act
alarming failure to realize that the consciousness of their own good intentions is not an adequate safeguard for the liberties of the people of Canada.
Then in the Calgary Herald of March 1, 1951, I find this statement:
We are not suggesting that the present government in Ottawa has any intention of using these emergency powers in the same way.
It was referring there to the way in which the German Reichstag took over emergency powers after it had been elected under a democratic procedure. The Calgary Herald continues:
But the democratic process, and still more the freedoms which that process enshrines, is a more delicate plant than we generally realize; and freedoms once surrendered are singularly hard to win back.
Then after further discussion of this subject it goes on:
But the chief criticism of the emergency powers bill is that it is altogether too general. It pretends to be specific while in fact it is nothing of the kind. It seems to us that if the government wants emergency powers in certain fields, then the necessary legislation ought to define those fields with absolute precision, the government ought to state in writing exactly what powers it proposes to use and how it proposes to use them, and if the government needs wider powers later on, then it should have to come back to parliament and get them by due process.
Mr. Speaker, in terms that are clear and understandable, the Calgary Herald was saying exactly the same thing as was said by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
Then there was another paper which was discussing this subject at the same time. I quote from the Montreal Gazette of March 5, 1951:
An emergency is a proper time for wide powers in the hands of the government. But it is also a proper time for wide powers in the hands of the courts. The present bill at Ottawa has the dangerous feature of establishing power at the expense of the courts.
The time when our liberties must be defended seems a poor time in which to undermine their essential guarantees.
Mr. Speaker, those were statements by responsible publications of different points of view and from different parts of Canada. Then I perhaps might properly quote the words used in a discussion which took place at the annual meeting of the advisory council of the National Liberal Federation of Canada in Ottawa on Tuesday, February 27, of last year. At that time Professor J. A. Corry, who is professor of political science at Queen's university, was discussing this very subject, and I quote briefly from what he had to say:
The discretionary powers exercised by our government nowadays in time of peace are wide enough to cause concern. The practical certainty of


cold war, if not actual shooting war, for an indefinite period means a still further substantial increase in the powers of the dominion government. What is our answer to Abraham Lincoln's question: Is a government which is strong enough to deal with serious crises not also going to be too strong for the liberties of its citizens?
Then Professor Corry went on to say much the same as has been said by some of the others to whom I have referred, to the effect that confidence in individuals is not in itself enough. He went on to say this:
If, as seems likely, we are to have a considerable measure of order in council government again, we should also be considering seriously the establishment of one or more committees of parliament to examine, not the substance and policy of the orders in council but the effect that the powers and procedures contained in them will have on individual rights and freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, it was quite clear that Professor Corry was suggesting exactly what Lord Hewart of Bury was pointing out earlier, namely that to the extent that administrative law must be exercised, it must also be brought under some measure of control, such as does not now exist; some measure of supervision by parliament before the event, not after; some measure of control which will make it possible for parliament to express its opinion before the government has taken its decision in a manner that would make any challenge of that decision an expression of want of confidence.
Mr. Speaker, I have put forward arguments made in this house, in the press and even at a meeting of the National Liberal Federation last year, in order to lay the foundation for the suggestion that the government itself might well consider at this time the abandoning of this legislation and the statement that it will deal with these matters by such legislation as may be required from time to time. If, as the Prime Minister says, the need is not very apparent for legislation of this kind immediately, and it has not been necessary for the government to use it very much, that is all the more reason why we should return to normal procedure;-and it is the Prime Minister who indicated that this is not the normal constitutional procedure

 all the more reason why we should return to the proper division of authority between the dominion and provincial governments, at a time that our whole federal constitution is under strain; all the more reason that we should return to the principles upon which this country became one nation in 1867.
I have put forward arguments which in no way can be disposed of as being arguments from this side of the house which might conceivably be put forward with some idea of embarrassing the government, as is so

often suggested whenever we make an argument which is not entirely in accord with the view expressed by the government itself.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has referred to the act, but let no one be in any doubt that this act does confer almost unlimited powers upon the government of Canada, not upon an individual group of men who, no matter how much we may wish them long lives and happiness are, in the words of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), not gifted with immortality. We are dealing with the law as an abstract question. We are dealing with an act which confers upon the government certain powers, and which in no place says it is this Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), this Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or this Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), even if all the confidence expressed in them by members on the other side were fully justified and were shared more generally throughout the house than may sometimes be apparent.
Let us see exactly what this act does permit the government to do. It permits it to do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations as the governor in council may, by reason of the existing international emergency, deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the governor in council shall extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated; then that section of the act sets out the following:
(a)	control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs;
(b)	control of communications and means of communication;
(c)	control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels;
(d)	transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;
(e)	trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture; and
(f)	imposition and recovery, in connection with any scheme of control, of fees or charges payable to the Receiver General of Canada or into any fund or account established by order or regulation for the purposes of the scheme of control.
Where is there any specific definition such as was requested by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), such as asked for by Lord Hewart of Bury, the great exponent of common law and parliamentary procedure? Where is there the specific provision asked for before the National Liberal Federation last year? Where is the specific provision asked for by leading writers in the press of this country? There 55704-162
Emergency Powers Act is none. Neither is there any specific definition of powers, nor is there any suggestion as to which minister shall exercise these powers.
It is true that there is some suggestion of restraint in subsection 2 of section 2 where it says:
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained therein, the powers conferred on the governor in council by subsection one do not include power to make orders or regulations in relation to
(a)	arrest, except as incidental to proceedings under section three, detention, exclusion or deportation of any person;
(b)	censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings; or
(c)	expenditure of moneys otherwise than in accordance with an appropriation by parliament except expenditure of moneys from any fund or account established by order or regulation in connection with a scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control.
Never was a reservation with more illusory protection put before this or any other house with a similar measure of authority and responsibility than the one now before us. It does seem that last year, very conscious of the grave situation with which we were confronted and the uncertainty as to how that grave situation was to be met-an uncertainty which may not be greater today, although the general situation is quite as grave and perhaps more grave-there may have been some tendency not to examine these things in the way they should now be examined when, with all the dangers, at least we have found some pattern of continuing action through the long period of emergency which lies ahead.
When this act says there shall be no provisions in regard to arrest except as incidental to proceedings under section 3, then we refer to section 3 and find that by order in council the government may prescribe penalties by way of fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years. This section is wide open in regard to determining what those powers shall be, and that is a very illusory protection. Section 3 does deal with seizure, detention, and forfeiture of goods by order in council, so the protection afforded in that section is not very satisfactory.
Then mention is made of censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings. There might be some protection there, except for the fact that this government has such control over newsprint today that if it saw fit-again I am dealing with the government of Canada and not the individual-under its present powers it could very effectively deal with any newspaper.

Do not let the Minister of Justice or anyone else in this house be so naive as to suggest that allocation is not a very powerful weapon at the present time, whether it be of newsprint or anything else.
Then we have paragraph (c) of subsection 2, which deals with the expenditure of moneys otherwise than in accordance with appropriation by parliament, except the expenditure of moneys from some fund set up under this order in council. I cannot imagine, Mr. Speaker, that this government would find it very difficult to conceive of a plan for some fund, if they really wanted to set up something outside of any ordinary appropriation, which would give them the financial resources they needed, even if they felt themselves under restraint, which I have not seen particularly noticeable in some of the items that have come up by way of supplementary estimates.
Whatever the reservations are, they are contained in these very limited terms. Otherwise wide open powers are given. The Prime Minister has made it quite clear that these powers do abridge the constitution, that these powers do change the plan of responsibility and authority in existence as between the dominion and the provincial governments under the British North America Act. Last year we pointed out that, with full recognition of all the dangers that exist, we opposed the bill on the ground that no argument had been presented which justified this immense delegation of power, especially in a time that the government still prefers to describe as a period of general peace. I am not quarrelling with the government in the use of that expression, but if the government is going to employ that expression then let it act in accordance with the expression it chooses to use. If we are to conduct ourselves as far as possible as though we were going to live reasonably normal lives over a long period of years, under the pressures of the international situation which now exist, most certainly we should try to carry on our system of government and our parliamentary, procedures in a manner which continues the traditional practices that have been built up over the centuries.
Whatever may have been said at that time last year, this house should not renew this act

Emergency Powers Act type of production that cannot be taken over by the government, if it sees fit to do so.
Do not dismiss that by saying that this government would not exercise such powers. There were those in other countries who supported laws of a similar nature and who today have lost all freedom as a result of the expressed belief that the governments of those countries would not abuse the power conferred upon them.
No, there would be no doubt here about the power of the government to seize any industry or to take over any operation. Under this no question would arise in connection with the nationalization of trucking, the nationalization of shipping or the nationalization of railways, if the government wanted to do it. Of course that is the qualification. But it is there in express terms-
Transportation by land, air or water, and the control of the transport of persons and things-
-by land, sea or air.
I do not know where there are such wide powers today in any country that still calls itself a democracy.

speechtext:
Oh, this act is much less explicit than the act passed in a time of war and which it replaces. Even in a time of war the government felt there was some necessity to give some appearance of defining powers and specifying subjects to an extent that does not appear in this measure at all. And may I say to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) that I am not suggesting for one moment that these powers were wisely conferred at that time, except under the impact of war itself; not merely because of the necessity of fighting the war but because of the impact of the events of war upon the daily lives of our people. That is one of the reasons such emergency powers as were introduced here, and were continued with some reservations, were accepted. People recognized that there were great limitations upon the daily activities of our people. No one will question those limitations, which are not now imposed upon the people, and which the government has wisely or unwisely refused most emphatically even to consider, though in some cases there were some who thought this might have been done with advantage to the people of Canada.
In that respect I would point out that one of the chief reasons given for the introduction of the measure last year was the possibility that the government might be called upon to exercise price control. The government now makes it clear that it has no intention of

doing so, so that argument has lost its validity, and is disposed of as a reason for the continuance of the measure, even if it ever represented a sound argument.
This discussion might well remind us that there was a very interesting point raised in the argument presented before the supreme court of the United States. I cannot help feeling that there was historic significance in the fact that counsel arguing the case there against the exercise of such powers as were exercised by the President of the United States cited section 39 of Magna Carta, which reads as follows:
No Freeman shall be taken, or imprisoned, or disseized, or outlawed, or exiled, or in any way harmed, nor will we go upon or send upon him, save by the lawful judgment of his peers, or by the law of the land.
Section 39 of Magna Carta is one of those great sections in the charter of our freedom signed at Runnymede in 1215. And there are two more provisions in that section which I submit should be in the minds of hon. members at this time when they consider delegating their responsibility in this manner to the government, without any defining restraint. There is the provision, first of all, that no freeman shall be disseized without the decision of his peers, and that no man shall be taken or imprisoned or disseized, except by the law of the land.
The act before us, in the powers it confers, denies the right assured by Magna Carta. It is not an answer to say, "Oh, no; this government would not exercise them." This government is creating those powers; this government is creating a precedent which others will find extremely convenient if at some distant time in the future there should be those in power who would believe in a much greater exercise of authority by the state than this government has demonstrated, great though its belief in its own omniscience and its own power has been.
