Mr. Speaker, I accord to the hon. member for Spadina considerable knowledge of the law. I hope he will impart some of that knowledge to one hon. member opposite, when he has the freedom to do so.
I do not think this is a strictly academic subject. I think it is time for hon. members to be as careful about the provisions of

Magna Carta as are some of our friends in the United States; to assert our belief in those principles, and to assert our belief that, except under the most express terms and the most explicit safeguards, there shall be no departure from that historic section of Magna Carta.
Ever since those days that fundamental principle has always been observed. It has been challenged, it has been denied, but in turn the people have overridden that denial. It was the denial of that right that brought a king of England to the block. It was the denial of that right that lost another king his throne. It was the denial of that right that lost to the British crown the provinces which constitute what is now the United States. It was the denial of that right that over and over again has challenged the great legal brains in this house as well as elsewhere. It was the possibility of the denial of that right that challenged one of the best parliamentary brains in this house, and I am referring to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).
I submit that without questioning the good faith but simply examining this as a matter of principle, the issue is clear and it goes to the root of democracy itself. Where law ends, tyranny begins. When it will begin, no one can tell. Others in other lands were very sure it would never begin, but today they have no right to raise their voices and point out that when they supported arbitrary laws of this nature they relied upon the government never to exercise its power.
The protection of our people must depend upon the rule of law provided by the people's representatives. The law itself must ever be a declaration of the people's representatives in parliament. If there is to be a real democracy in this or any other country then the laws must be made by those elected to make them and not by the executive sitting behind closed doors under a delegation of powers such as is contained in this act.
If our parliamentary system is to survive through the vicissitudes of the years ahead, then our laws must be the expression of the will of the community as approved by the elected representatives of the whole community. Our people have the right to know what the law is at any given time; and before they are bound by laws they should have concurred in the adoption of those laws through their own decisions in parliament before the laws were passed, not after they had been passed and were in effect.
The rule of law is the rule of freedom. Men have the right to know to what extent their representatives have said they must obey certain injunctions. Even then there may still be doubt; as we all know, competent
Emergency Powers Act lawyers often give conflicting advice on different points of view. We have just recently seen a case where the Supreme Court of Canada held a different view from that of the privy council, although of course the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) believes that we should not in any way rely upon the privy council. Without in any way questioning the confidence he has expressed, this indicates that very competent judges, let alone very competent lawyers, may hold diametrically opposed views as to the effect of orders in council. subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE OF SECTIONS ONE TO THREE UNTIL MAY 30, 1953
speechtext:
The orders in council were so loosely drawn that there was never any question about it from the beginning. That was one of the points upon which the whole argument rested at various stages throughout the long proceedings. I may assert without any question that they were extremely loosely drawn and that was what presented the difficulty from the very beginning. Nevertheless the privy council has now made it perfectly clear that if any parliament is to delegate wide powers, then those wide powers can be exercised in a manner which the courts will be most reluctant to limit in any way. With that judgment of the privy council we are much less safe in passing these sweeping powers than we were while we still had the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada. I might have preferred the judgment of the Supreme Court of

Emergency Powers Act Canada; the Minister of Justice prefers the privy council. The Minister of Justice has that judgment, but that judgment is a warning to every one of us that we should be careful as to what powers we confer upon this government. The previous judgment did suggest that there might be some restraint exercised by the court.
The Minister of Justice may well emphasize to us the expression known as the glorious uncertainty of the law. He exemplifies it. Nevertheless there is a difference between that glorious uncertainty of the law which is common to all legal proceedings- that is what I have sought to emphasize; it is not only the Minister of Justice, but I pointed out the glorious uncertainty as between the Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council-and the certainty that no one is going to know what the law is until it finally emerges some time much later from the star chamber where it has been adopted by the government. That kind of law passed into disrepute centuries ago and it should be disposed of by this house at this time.
There can be no security if laws are uncertain and if people do not know in advance what the views of justice really are going to be. Strong arguments were presented against this bill when it was introduced. I should like to refer to what was said a year ago because I want to leave no doubt as to our position in regard to this act, and to show that it has been consistent in regard to the principle which is in issue. I should like to quote from page 952 of Hansard of March 6, 1951, where in regard to this very measure I am reported as saying:
To the statement that I have just made the Prime Minister can answer that this bill will terminate next year.
I went on to discuss how bills of this kind have a habit of being repeated, of being renewed and of becoming embedded in our ordinary practices and procedures. Then I went on to say:
The Prime Minister may also say: This is in the hands of parliament. In answer I would say that we have not seen too much evidence, during this session or preceding ones, that there is that measure of independent expression of opinion by the large number of supporters of the government in this house which would suggest to those who are concerned about the trend we now see that we might hope that within this house there would be a vote which would place any effective restraint upon a government which commanded a majority of that kind. Unless we return to established and tested principles of parliamentary democracy we may in fact at this hour be in the twilight of freedom here in Canada, no matter how much we believe in freedom itself. We Canadians can pay the penalty of surrender just as other people have paid the penalty of surrender of those principles which protected the freedom in which they believed.

I repeat these words but with a greater sense of urgency today, because none of the arguments that could have been presented at that time can properly be put forward now in support of this measure. Assuming the utmost good will in the mind of the government, the fact remains that it is the duty of every one of us to consider what could happen if men of evil intention had the opportunity to exercise the powers conferred by such an act. That is the only test which can properly be applied to legislation of this kind. Freedom has disappeared so often in recent years When that test was not applied. Examining only what could be done and not what any of us might suggest would be done by this particular government, I do not see how anyone can deny that a full and unlimited exercise of the powers contained in this act could become the death warrant of democracy in Canada.
At a time when we are seeking to preserve the spirit, the form, the living body and the traditions of democracy, I most earnestly urge the government to withdraw this resolution. It can withdraw it in the same way that it has on other occasions when other measures have been presented and the government became convinced that it was not desirable to proceed. That does not mean it cannot deal with any cases which it thinks should be dealt with. It is only necessary for the government to examine what was done during the past year under this act and anything that conceivably could be required during the coming year, and then introduce simple amendments to existing legislation which will permit them to deal with the matter under clearly defined and limited terms.
May I also say that, if circumstances should arise short of war which call for wider powers, we have seen that this parliament can meet within a few days and pass whatever laws are necessary. In the event that the most unhappy possibility of war should become a reality the government need not be concerned because it has the powers already.
I hope these arguments will not be brushed aside with the suggestion that this government would never consider doing anything so improper as the possibilities that might be presented. I only ask the government to examine with care the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), by an expert on constitutional law who spoke before the National Liberal Federation in Ottawa, by Lord Hew-art of Bury whom I am sure the lawyers of this house respect, and by others outside of the house, as well as the great lawyers

and jurists of Canada; and without taking any argument from the opposition I think they would come to the conclusion that the delegation of power of this kind is extremely unwise.
Members of the house who are lawyers remember well that in a democracy we only exercise on behalf of the people the powers delegated to us by the people themselves. Every lawyer in the house remembers that ancient Latin maxim, delegatus non potest delegare. We only have power delegated to us by the people of Canada, and it is not our right to delegate to the executive meeting behind closed doors the business of the people of Canada which has been entrusted to us under our free democratic processes. Therefore in these times, which the government is finding sufficiently normal to deal with so many things in what they regard as a normal manner, may I urge that they return to normal. May I recall what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself said. He made it clear that this legislation departs from the normal constitutional procedure of the House of Commons. He made it clear that this legislation destroys the constitutional balances between the dominion and provincial governments. I am only asking, with respect, that all members on both sides of the house give due consideration to the importance of asserting their belief in the Canadian constitution at this great testing time for democracy throughout the whole world.

Mr. Speaker, when the Emergency Powers Act was before parliament in the first session of 1951 we in this group supported it. We did so because we recognized the existence of an emergency and because we felt that, in addition to steps that might have to be taken to meet that emergency from a defence point of view, there were also steps that might have to be taken from an economic point of view. Indeed, we argued very strongly at that time that the Canadian people were suffering because of rising prices and a lowering of their real standards of living. We argued that the institution of a system of price controls and subsidies, where necessary, was required. We supported the Emergency Powers Act in the realization that it would make possible the institution of such controls, and we urged the government as strongly as we could to take advantage of the right which parliament was conferring on them in order to protect the interests of the Canadian people.
In our view a state of emergency still exists. In fact we are not sure that it has lessened from what it was a year ago. The
Emergency Powers Act state of military activity in Korea may be different from what it was then, but the situation is as explosive as ever not only there and throughout the Far East, but in other parts of the world. For example, we in this group are concerned over what is being done this very day with respect to the taking of a step which in our view divides Germany into two armed camps. What may flow from that step is a matter of conjecture which it is not too pleasant to contemplate, but I mention it at this time merely to indicate that in our view the world situation is still one of emergency.
The economic situation is likewise still one of emergency so far as our people at home are concerned. The government has boasted over the fact that the cost of living index may have dropped a fraction of a point, but the plain fact of the matter is that the cost of living is still beyond the reach of the workers and farmers of this country who are producing the nation's wealth in terms of a gross national product in excess of anything that we have known in our history. And yet our people are suffering because they cannot afford to buy the goods they produce. That to us is a ridiculous situation, and in our view it is still important that certain direct economic controls should be instituted.
We firmly believe that man was not made for economic orders but that economic orders are supposed to be made for man. We do not believe in submitting our people to the suffering that comes from the play and the control of blind economic forces. We believe it is consistent with, and is a part of, the whole principle of democracy that our people should control not just a limited sphere of the things that concern us but should control completely that which concerns our people perhaps most of all, namely economic affairs. We believe that to leave these things to blind economic forces is to accept economic anarchy.
Because this measure which the government asks to be continued for another year not only would make it possible for the government to deal, within certain limitations, with emergencies of a defence nature but also with the economic emergencies that our people are facing in this country, we take the same view we took when the same bill was before the house in 1951. We shall support the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the continuation of this act for a period of another twelve months.
Had it not been for the very long speech to which we have just listened-and hon. members are, I am sure, glad to know that the rules of the house prevent me from speaking at the same length-

When we assert our concern for parliamentary democracy and when at the same time we accept the fact that we are in a state of emergency, does it not become necessary for us to find some sort of balance, to find some way to make our parliamentary way of doing things fit the needs of the emergency in which we find ourselves? It was because this legislation, when it was brought down a year ago, was an attempt to find that balance that we are prepared to accept its continuance for another year.
May I point out that the legislation which was brought down a year ago did not pass this house in the exact form in which it was first presented. Proposals were made on the floor of the house and some suggestions came from members of the Progressive Conservative group, some from our group and some from others. parliament over the government in its use of the powers conferred upon the government by this statute.
At this point I might perhaps deal with one of the most important elements of protection which we won from the government on that occasion. I may say that when the government put that section in the bill it was an innovation. It was a provision that we did not have in the War Measures Act or in the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act and that sort of legislation we had after the war. Here, for the first time in Canadian legislation, we had the counterpart of something which has been in existence at Westminster, namely a provision that the Senate and the House of Commons could, by resolution, annul or rescind any of the orders passed under this act. It was on the basis of that undertaking that we accepted this measure last year as being one that gave parliament a clear-cut and definite way of annulling any order passed under this act, if parliament felt that such should be done. I submit that for that undertaking to be repeated today, as the Prime Minister has done, is to cope with this situation in the best possible way.
Not only does the act provide for annulment of regulations or orders that may be passed by the government, but it does impose very definite limitations on the fields in which orders can be passed. Likewise, the act was limited last year in that it was to expire as of May 31 this year, subject to the possibility of it being continued for only one more year. The motion we now have before us takes advantage of that provision, but there is no provision anywhere in the act for it being continued any further after the end of May, 1953. Thus there are very definite limitations in this legislation, and I suggest that to speak of this as going 55704-1G3
Emergency Powers Act back to star chamber methods, as surrendering the rights of parliament and all the rest of it, is indeed using extravagant language.
Perhaps the strongest point the leader of the opposition makes is that he does not like merely to have the opportunity to pass upon laws after they have been given effect by the governor in council. I agree that I do not like that having to be done, even under ordinary legislation. But if we are going to admit it is an emergency situation, we have to give some responsibility to the government. May I point out that there are other measures, namely the taxation changes which take place, year by year, which become effective before parliament has the right to pass upon them. Parliament, however, still has the right to negate those changes if it wishes to do so. We still have the right under this act to negate, annul or rescind any of these regulations which the government might introduce. As I say, Mr. Speaker, this is a line of argument that I did not expect to use at all in my remarks today, but speaking on behalf of a group which is deeply concerned over parliamentary procedure as well as over parliamentary democracy and the rights of the members of this house to represent the people, it did seem necessary to deal with some of these arguments that the leader of the opposition has put forward.
The leader of the opposition is concerned about the rule of law. He came back to that phrase time and time again. I do not see the relevance of the argument. We are not saying to the government that it can pass any kind of laws it wants. We are giving the government certain limited powers, and we spell out those powers. We make it clear also that they can be effective for only a limited period of time. We require that any regulations or orders passed under this act shall be given publicity, and shall be tabled in parliament within a certain period of time. It seems to me that, all told, not too bad a job is being done in dealing with the problem of an emergency situation.
If we want the government to accept its responsibility to deal with the emergency situation on the defence side, if we in this group in particular want the government to deal with economic problems that face our people and want, as we do, the institution of price controls and the payment of subsidies to help our people cope with the cost of living, we have no alternative but to confer upon that government some means by which they can carry out the things we ask them to do.

Emergency Powers Act
We have had today, as we have had so often, the argument about the British North America Act and the whole question of the division of jurisdiction between the federal government and the provincial governments. I shall not take time to go into that at length. We still feel as a former colleague of ours, the late Frank Jaenicke, used to point out so well, that there was real validity in the judgment of the privy council in the Canada Temperance Act case. I refer to the judgment in which their lordships said that any question, which by its inherent nature was tied in with the welfare of the whole of Canada, was a subject upon which the parliament of Canada could legislate. We have in mind as well the decisions that have been made by the courts to the effect that when parliament in its wisdom declares a state of emergency, it is not for the courts to look behind that declaration. We believe there is a state of emergency. The leader of the opposition believes that. He tried to say it was less severe than it was a year ago, yet at one time during his remarks he said it was as grave as a year ago or perhaps even more grave.
Because of these constitutional arguments I have put forward, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we are quite within our rights, as a federal parliament, in passing legislation of this kind. I go further and suggest it is not merely a question of whether or not we are within our rights. Indeed, as a federal parliament we have certain responsibilities to the people of Canada. Our responsibility to them at this time of international crisis, and at this time of economic crisis in our own country, is to set up the machinery to enable the govem-ment-which at all times is responsible to this parliament and we will always hold them to that responsibility-to deal with this crisis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks before six o'clock I think I made it clear that we were not impressed by the arguments used by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in opposing the motion now before the house.
We of this group supported this legislation a year ago, and we feel it is desirable that it should be continued for another year. Nevertheless we wish to make it clear that we are not satisfied with the record of the government in its use of the powers conferred by this legislation. Our complaint against the government is not that they have used


these powers too freely but that they have not used them for the purposes to which many people in this country hoped they would be put when this legislation was brought into parliament a year ago.
The people of Canada have not suffered from abuses under the Emergency Powers Act. The people of Canada have suffered because of the failure of the government to use these powers to control prices and protect the living standards of the Canadian people. In supporting the continuance of this legislation we do so in the hope that the government will reconsider the whole question of its attitude toward prices, and toward economic controls. The people of this country still believe it is their right to expect from the government protection of their living standards, particularly when it is because of a time of crisis, and when it is to a large extent because of defence spending that we are experiencing inflation as we are at the present time. So, Mr. Speaker, we give our support to this legislation; we turn aside the arguments against it, as I sought to do in my remarks before six o'clock, but we call upon the government to make better use of this legislation in the interests of the people of Canada during the twelve months that lie ahead than has been the case during the twelve months that have just gone by.
When the Prime-Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke this afternoon he gave an account of the government's stewardship under this legislation. He is to be commended for having told us the whole story of the number of orders passed under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act; but I thought as he gave that list, particularly when he recounted the last five to which he referred, that it must have been apparent to him that to a certain extent this legislation had been used as a matter of convenience. Indeed, the last five which the Prime Minister discussed were hardly measures that could be described as matters of emergency. He admitted it was simply a case of using this legislation to deal with these matters until such time as there could be appropriate legislation.
It is our contention that in giving these powers to the government parliament is not simply giving the government a convenient way of dealing with ordinary matters; parliament is giving the government power to deal with extraordinary matters. The extraordinary situation, both on the defence front and in terms of economic matters here at home, is the reason for legislation of this kind. We support the legislation, but we call upon the government to make use of it in the interests of the Canadian people.

The following address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada:
To His Excellency the Kight Honourable Vincent Massey, Member of the Order of the Companions of Honour, Governor General, and Commander in Chief of Canada.
May it please Your Excellency:
We, Her Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, respectfully approach Your Excellency, praying that the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act be continued in force until the thirty-first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-four.
He said: On May 5 I informed the house that an order in council had been passed effective May 6, revoking the regulations under the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act. I also stated that the government would during the present session invite both houses of parliament to present addresses to the Governor General praying that the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act be continued for a further period.
The act was passed by parliament in September, 1950, and authorized the governor in council to make regulations concerning the control of consumer credit. At that time inflationary pressures were building up rapidly all over the world, and were a cause for serious concern to all of us in this house. There had been a very rapid expansion of consumer credit during 1950. Further expansion of this type of consumer buying would have added to these upward pressures on prices.
The first consumer credit regulations under the authority of the act were passed by order in council October 25, 1950, and became effective November 1, 1950. Under these regulations a down payment of 33J per cent was required for motor vehicles and 20 per cent for other consumer goods. The minimum down payment and monthly payment were 55704-163i
Consumer Credit Act
each $5, and the maximum period of payment 18 months. In the early part of 1951 the effects of inflation upon the price level became much more pronounced and in March the regulations were sharply stiffened by raising the down payment to 50 per cent for motor vehicles and 33J per cent for other consumer goods, by raising both the minimum down payment and monthly payment to $10, and by reducing the maximum period of payment to 12 months. In January of this year the regulations were relaxed by extending the maximum period of payment to 18 months, and finally the regulations were revoked effective May 6 when it was felt that the need for them had passed.
There is no way of measuring the exact effect of consumer credit control over this period. But the statistics show that cash sales of durable goods expanded more rapidly during the first few months of 1951 than did instalment sales, a reversal of the situation in 1950 when the consumer credit regulations were not in force. There can be very little doubt that combined with the government's other anti-inflationary measures they were of considerable importance in first limiting and then levelling off the upward spiral of prices. Perhaps the best evidence of their effectiveness lies in the volume of requests we received for their removal or relaxation.
At present the direct limitation of consumer credit seems not to be necessary. Preliminary indications are that the total of consumer credit outstanding as at March 31 of this year was less than a year ago in spite of higher average prices and incomes. Nevertheless we must remind ourselves that the economy is still subject to some very heavy demand and that we have not yet reached the peak of our defence program. The international situation is still uncertain, and we must be in a position to deal promptly with unexpected events. While the probabilities are against a renewal of inflationary forces as powerful as those which beset us in late 1950 and early 1951, we cannot ignore the possibility. Defence expenditure is still increasing, projected capital investment for the current year is above last year's level and incomes are high and rising. It would not take much to upset the balance. If such a situation should1 develop we should not hesitate to reintroduce credit controls, but the effectiveness of any such measures depends upon their prompt application.
The consumer credit act, as originally passed by parliament, was given a two-year term of life, with a proviso that it could be extended for a further period of life on the presentation

Consumer Credit Act
of addresses from this house and from the Senate. The government recommends that the act be extended for a further period of two years, that is until July 31, 1954. This date coincides approximately with the time set for the achievement of our present defence program, and therefore covers the logical period during which the government should have these special powers.
It is with these considerations in mind that I move the address for the extension of the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act for a further period of two years. I think there is a good chance that we shall not need to use the authority which such an extension of the act would grant. I hope that this will be the case not only because such restraints are naturally irksome to both buyers and sellers, but because the necessity of again resorting to such restraint would mean that the general relative stability which now prevails had been seriously disturbed. But the possibility that control of consumer credit may again become necessary in the course of the next two years cannot be ignored, and if the necessity arises the measures to be taken will be more effective and can be less drastic if they can be applied quickly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have here a resolution proposing that a measure passed in the autumn of 1950 known as the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act be extended for two years. I draw attention immediately to the fact that it is proposed1 that this be extended for two years, whereas the Prime Minister's resolution moved this afternoon was for an extension of one year only. I shall revert to that, because it seems to me it is very difficult to make an argument for two years in this case, as against one year in the other. I shall suggest in an amendment that the term be reduced to one year.
I should like now to make a few general observations about the act itself. We remember very well the situation in the autumn of 1950, when we came back for a short session. We remember that at that time the war news from Korea was very bad, and that the defence spending spurt which had taken place during the summer had produced an inflationary situation, which the minister has described, and which in fact led to the initiation of the measure passed in the autumn of 1950.
At that time, as I think the minister himself more or less conceded in his following budget speech of April, 1951, the regulations had very little by way of teeth in them. Actually they had done little or nothing to improve the situation by the time of the budget speech in 1951.

Indeed, it was worse than that, because the whole action of the government during the autumn and winter of 1950-51 was to stimulate rather than to curb spending. As a matter of fact we all remember the spending splurge that took place at that time which, to some extent, was due to the fact that the government had created a feeling that there were likely to be shortages, without really having taken any worth-while steps to curb spending. And so we had that tremendous splurge.
Then we came along to the first session of 1951, when the situation was getting rapidly out of hand. We had1 then the interesting speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in which he told us so vividly and so frankly that the situation really, in a sense, had got largely out of hand. As he described it, the people who were in the business of selling goods had got themselves, in his words, "all set", and he thought at that time very little could be done about it.
Well, very little was done about it until the situation got bad. As we know, it went on for many months. And then with, I think, some assistance from this measure, which was tightened up and given more teeth in the spring of 1951, the situation has for the moment steadied. The minister has given us a picture of that. At the same time he feels he should be armed with this weapon, in case it is necessary to use it again.
I shall not take much of the time of the house to recall the unfortunate situation that developed. We had in the autumn of 1950, just after the Korean debacle, a situation where too little was done. Then in the spring of 1951 we had the minister's drastic taxation measures, which we all remember very well. My own guess, and I think it is more than a guess, is that the improvement in the military situation which took place in Korea immediately after the adjournment of the session in the autumn of 1950, eased the minds of the ministry-perhaps particularly the mind of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-so that, as I say, little was done during the winter. In fact what was done was actually inimical to the situation.
Then in the spring of 1951 we had the taxes, which have been so fully discussed- taxes which bore so heavily on certain of the industries, including the motor car industry and others. At the same time heavier taxes were introduced, stronger teeth were put into the instalment buying provisions. So the two things went along together until we had this very, very unsatisfactory situation during the last year, which the minister has striven to cure by backing away from his consumer controls, and removing them until

we are given to understand, at any rate it is common gossip, that deferred depreciation will also go by the boards.
My feeling about this is that it is a device which has been badly used. At the same time, with the possibility of heavy buying and further inflation I dislike to go the length of opposing it entirely. I content myself therefore, at the moment, with moving that the two-year period be reduced to one year. There is no reason whatever why the period should be two years. If we give an extra year we can take stock of the situation when the twelve months have expired just as we intend to do in connection with the Emergency Powers Act. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton):
That the word "fifty-three" be substituted for the word "fifty-four" where the latter appears in the resolution.
In other words, that the extension of the act be for one year and not for two.

As the house knows this is a matter of considerable interest to the civil service and other workers in this country, and has been discussed a good deal of late. As hon. members know, with regard to the
Public Service-Five-day week civil service the matter of the five-day week has been presented to the government in various ways and various answers have been given on different occasions. Recently the indication has been that the Minister of Finance is prepared to meet representatives of the civil service at an early date to discuss this matter. In the meantime a number of statements have been made which suggest that the minister's mind is somewhat made up already. My purpose in taking advantage of this opportunity to speak on a grievance is to express the hope that when the minister meets the representatives of the civil service he will meet them with an open mind.
The fact of the matter is that quite a number of people employed by the government now have a five-day week. Therefore in asking for a five-day week for the civil service we are not making a request for something brand new. I think the minister realizes from what I have just said that I am speaking about employees of other emanations of the crown and agencies of the government apart from the civil service. As I say, there are a number of employees in that category who are on the five-day week.
This is shown by sessional paper 180 which was tabled in the House of Commons on April 21, 1952, having been brought down in response to some questions of mine which were passed as an order for return on November 28, 1951. This sessional paper indicates the following employees in the following organizations as being on the five-day week, and it shows the number in each case:
Bank of Canada	 1,186
Canadian Arsenals Ltd	 3'27l
' Canadian Broadcasting Corporation	 L300
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation l'<)44

This sessional paper also indicates that employees of Canadian National Railways, Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, Canadian wheat board and Trans-Canada Air Lines are also on the five-day week although the return does not give the number of employees in these cases. I believe the same holds true for employees of the national research council and of the defence research board.
Another interesting return was tabled on Wednesday, May 21, 1952, being sessional paper 113C. This was brought down in answer to questions asked by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who inquired specifically as to whether the five-day week was in effect in any department of government, any crown corporation or government agency and, if so, what departments, corporations or agencies.

Public Service-Five-day week
The sessional paper is rather bulky, being made up of some 33 pages, but as one goes through it he finds that in addition to government employees outside of the civil service, to whom I have already referred, who are now enjoying the five-day week, there are quite a number of civil servants as such who are also enjoying the five-day week. In particular it appears from this return that practically all civil servants in the Toronto district are now on the five-day week. I need not take up the time of the house to go through this return page by page, but it includes answers from the civil service commission and from quite a number of departments which indicate that practically all the civil servants in the city of Toronto are on' the five-day week, and that there are some civil servants in special situations in other parts of the country who are likewise on that work period.
I understand that representations have been made to the government by civil servants in other precise localities. For example, civil servants in Windsor have asked that they be put on the five-day week in the same way as civil servants in Toronto. In other words we are not breaking new ground in making this request. We are not asking for an innovation. The five-day week is already in effect in a good many instances. In addition to the fact that there are such groups of people who are on the five-day week the year round, there are other departments of the government whose civil servants have enjoyed the five-day week during certain periods of the year, particularly in the summer on certain occasions. Despite all these facts which indicate some progress toward the five-day week, the government maintains an attitude of resistance toward representations that it should be extended and made really general in the civil service. The return from which I was quoting a few moments ago, sessional paper No. 180 of April 21, 1952, in addition to giving the factual information asked for also dealt with my fifth and sixth questions which were as follows:
5.	What consideration has been given to such representations?
6.	What progress is being made by the government in getting ready for the five-day week for all civil servants and all government employees?
The answers to these two questions were incorporated in one answer which is as follows:
The treasury board and its staff, the civil service commission and the national joint council of the public service have studied the developments and proposals relating to the five-day week in the light of other considerations bearing upon the possible adoption of it as a general policy. The five-day week has been adopted in certain units of the public service where it would promote efficiency and could be introduced without reduction in hours of work or service to the public and without increasing staff. In view of the need to economize in labour

and expenditure, and to secure maximum national productivity at this time of abnormal requirements arising from the defence program, the government has not, however, considered it desirable to adopt the five-day week for the civil service as a whole.
The government of course was not surprised when the publication of that answer was greeted with some disappointment by civil servants generally. In fact their representatives spoke rather strongly about the attitude of the government, particularly in view of the fact that not long before that sessional paper was tabled the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had said in the house in answer to a question of mine that the matter was being studied, that representations would be considered, and that it would not be necessary for all the different civil service organizations to make separate representations.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that included in these critical comments made by various civil service representatives were those which appeared in the May issue of one of their publications, the Canadian Civil Servant. There is a paragraph on page 7 which reads as follows:
Indicating an unwavering determination to see the institution of the short work week throughout the civil service he claimed-
The "he" refers to Fred Knowles.
-that its inauguration would result in a higher level of productivity, efficiency and morale than now exists.
It is that sort of approach that I plead with the Minister of Finance to consider. In my view you cannot look at the question of the five-day week simply as a matter of ordinary cold mathematics. It is not a correct analysis of the situation to assume that if you cut down from five and a half days to five or from six days to five it automatically is going to mean a loss in productivity or a commensurate increase all across the board in other personnel. Beyond doubt there will be some cases where, in order to maintain public service six or seven days a week if necessary, additional people will have to be employed; but it seems to me there is no question but that in a large area of the government service there could be a reduction in the total number of days of work or total number of hours of work per week without lessening of production.
Indeed, you might even get an increase in production arising from a higher level of productivity, efficiency and morale than now exists. My plea to the Minister of Finance is that when he meets the representatives of the civil servants to discuss this matter he meet them with an open mind and consider

just such points as were made in the statement by Fred Knowles, to which I have just referred. As the minister knows, other representatives of civil servants have made similar statements.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that in addition to such progress as is being made in the government service in terms of the five-day week, it is becoming fairly general in Canada as a whole. On December 3, 1951 certain questions of mine regarding the five-day week were answered in Hansard at page 1510. My questions were these:
1.	Has the government any statistics as to the number of (a) industrial workers: (b) office workers now on (i) a five-day week; (ii) a five and a half day week; (iii) a six-day week?
2.	If so, what are the number of each of the above groups of workers who are working for each of the periods indicated above?
The answer given by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour is in the form of a table which I shall not endeavour to place upon Hansard again, but when the minister is getting ready to meet the civil servants I would ask him to look at the table on page 1510 of Hansard for December 3, 1951. I may say that I was pleasantly surprised myself, when these figures were given by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour, to discover the extent to which the five-day week is now the rule among industrial and office workers in Canada generally. I find from the table that in terms of plant workers there are 510,000 whose work week is more than five days, be it five and a half days, six days or whatever it may be, but there are 537,000 who are already on the five-day week. In terms of office workers, there are 81,000 who are on a work week of more than five days compared with 107,000 on the five-day week. In other words, the majority of both industrial and office workers are already on the five-day week. Incidentally, I asked specifically later on whether these figures included bank employees, quite a number of whom have since gone on the five-day week because of enabling legislation passed by parliament. I was informed that these figures did not include bank employees. In other words the situation is actually better than is indicated by the figures I have given.
The whole idea in advocating the five-day week is that with the increased productivity of our modern economy it is axiomatic that a share of that increased productivity should be passed on to those who produce the nation's wealth. You do that in various ways. You do it by the scale of wages, by the prices that you pay for farm products. You do it by social security and in various other ways. You also do it by reducing
Public Service-Five-day week the number of hours or days per week that people have to work, thus making it possible for people to enjoy a little more of the life that they are working to make possible. It is good to know that this trend is developing in Canada generally; but in my view there is still a long way to go, and I certainly feel that the federal government should give a stronger lead in this respect with regard to its own civil servants.
I want to say in passing that the federal government should also consider its own labour legislation with respect to the five-day week as it affects employees generally. For example, we have in this country the position that employees of Canadan Pacific hotels in some cases enjoy a shorter work week than do employees of Canadian National hotels. The reason is that, by a decision of the privy council, employees of the Canadian National hotels are regarded as coming under federal labour jurisdiction whereas employees	of	Canadian	Pacific	hotels	areregarded	as	coming	under	provinciallabour jurisdiction. In some of the provinces there are work-week laws that give to employees	of	Canadian	Pacific	hotels	theprotection	of	a shorter	work	week,	but
employees of Canadian National hotels are denied that protection because there is no such work-week limitation in federal legislation.
That is just in passing, Mr. Speaker, to point out that those of us who are concerned about the work week of our people are concerned about it on all fronts. My particular purpose in raising the matter at this time is to express the hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his officials who will go into this matter will consider it from all angles. Let them consider the extent to which government employees outside the civil service already have a five-day week. Let them face the fact that in Toronto, for example, civil servants already have the five-day week.

subtopic: FIVE-DAY WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the five-day week were granted, then the proposal would toe made that we must have a four-day week. It seems to me that we have lost sight of an important point with regard to the civil servants here in the great capital city of our nation. I am not one who would say whether they should have a five-day week, a six-day week or a seven-day week; but I would say that each hour they spend in their work should be spent profitably, happily and with enthusiasm, working for this great country.
Coming as I do from a far removed part of our nation, when I come to Ottawa I wonder that people live in such a circumscribed area. I find in the city of Ottawa today the same limits that were set when I was here as a boy forty years ago. I wonder whether, here in the city of Ottawa, there is not some kind of influence that is holding the limits of the city within narrow bounds with the hope of extracting from the civil servants the ultimate in rental for premises occupied. It is unfortunate that I should say this, but I know people in the civil service who are enjoying very small incomes and pay more for a suite than I could afford to pay, even with my income. They are limited to apartment houses, duplexes and so forth. They pay $100 and $125 a month for a suite whereas out in the Cariboo country we should be glad to have $10 a month for similar premises.
I have a suggestion which I am going to give the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). He is one of the younger members in this house, with a bright future before him, and in his heart he must have hope for the welfare of this nation. Ottawa is the brains of Canada. Within the boundaries of Ottawa, this capital, are the people who administer the affairs of Canada. Is it not therefore desirable that these civil servants should be given every opportunity to live full, happy and wholesome lives? I suggest that the Minister of Finance should start tonight to plot out a city for the future, a great subdivision that will extend from the Ottawa river right over to Prescott-it could be extended by degrees from time to time-in order to allow these people to get out of the heart of these purlieus and into the beautiful

countryside of Ontario; to get an acre or half an acre of land, with water laid down, sewers, hydro and paved streets. A man earning $150 a month could then go out 20 miles from this town and there live a good life, raise his family, and give them the advantages of school and church and other opportunities.
We live here in the midst of plenty. In fact I am reminded of the story of the man in the boat who was seeking fresh water and who said: Water, water everywhere and not a drop to drink. He was told: Drop your bucket on the other side and you will find there is lots of water.
We are here in the centre of eastern Ontario, with all this land in this productive valley of the Ottawa and the Rideau. No part of the world is more productive and more beautiful than this part of the country contiguous to Ottawa. Yet our stupid people allow a few real estate agents to confine the boundaries of the town within narrow limits. We should have a great highway from here to Prescott; it should be a four-lane highway. We should lay out subdivisions on either side of it where there would really be an opportunity to make homes for all our civil servants. No matter how small their incomes might be, they would share with us the free air, the good food, and good water and all the amenities of life to which every Canadian is entitled.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, TO GIVE POWER TO BOARD TO BORROW FROM MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
This resolution seeks authority to introduce a bill to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Act in order to bring the act more up to date, and make it a more flexible and efficient instrument for financing the mortgage requirements of Canadian farmers. The act was originally passed in 1927 and has not been amended since 1935. Conditions have altered substantially since that time, and it is desirable to make certain changes to enable the board to fulfil more effectively its function of providing mortgage credit for Canadian agriculture.
The most important amendments are designed to enlarge the board's field of operations by increasing the aggregate amount of loans which may be made to any one borrower on a first mortgage, and on a first and second mortgage together, by enabling the board to lend on a more generous scale in relation to the value of the security, and by adding to the purposes for which second mortgage loans may be made. At present the board cannot loan more than $5,000 on a first mortgage and $6,000 on a first and second mortgage together to any one borrower. The new bill will increase these limits to $10,000 and $12,000 respectively, that is $10,000 on the first mortgage to any one borrower or $12,000 on first and second mortgage combined to any one borrower. The reasons for this proposed amendment will be obvious. If lending
Canadian Farm Loan Act limits of $5,000 or $6,000 were reasonably sound in 1927 and 1934, the development of Canadian agriculture since that time, the rise in the value of farm land and in the cost of farm equipment and so on should make the proposed new limits not inappropriate.
The present act also limits a first mortgage loan to 50 per cent of the actual value of the land and buildings to be mortgaged, buildings being considered only to the extent to which they add to the actual value of the land as farm land. If a summer cottage is built on the farm, therefore, it is not eligible so far as valuation is concerned for lending purposes. Furthermore the act limits the aggregate of first and second mortgage loans to be made to any one borrower to two-thirds of the appraised value of land and buildings in provinces where chattel security may be taken, and to 60 per cent of the said value in provinces where chattel security cannot be taken. In the new bill authority is sought to increase the limit of a first mortgage loan to 60 per cent of the value of the security, and the limit of first and second mortgage taken together to 70 per cent of the value of the security in those provinces where chattel security may be taken, and to 65 per cent in those provinces where no chattel security can be taken. I think it will be generally agreed that the board has had a sound lending record, and this record has only been possible because it has not been unduly generous in the amount of credit it has extended or unwise in the selection of its risks. I do not think we wish the board to make unsound loans and become a burden on the general body of taxpayers, but I hope it will be agreed that the lending limits in relation to the board's appraised value of properties can now be raised, as the bill provides, without assuming an undue measure of risk.
The other way in which the scope of the board's operations is being enlarged is by extending the purposes for which second mortgage loans may be made. At present they cannot be used to purchase land, but I see no reason for this restriction and experience has shown that it can be safely removed, and wisely so in the general interest.
There are two other proposed amendments to which I may call special attention at this time. One provides for the establishment of a national advisory board to consider from time to time, discuss with the board and make recommendations to the board concerning the lending policies of the board, the principles underlying the valuation of farm property and the conditions affecting or that may affect lending policy on outstanding or future loans. At present there is provision

Canadian Farm Loan Act in the act for the setting up of local advisory boards, but this provision has not appeared to be practicable and has not been implemented. I hope the new provision may serve a useful purpose.
The second provision to which I shall call attention is one relating to the audit of the accounts of the board. At present this audit is in the hands of a private firm. Under the new bill which this resolution seeks authority to introduce, it is proposed to have the Auditor General of Canada act as the board's auditor. This change is, of course, in line with the general principles of our new Financial Administration Act.

The attitude of the board ought to be a little more generous; and there ought to be provision for a little loss. I do not suggest that we should encourage great losses or extravagances, but I would suggest to the minister that he should keep that in mind. I know the man who set this thing in motion. Up in our end of the country, north of the Peace river, very few loans have been made because of the unwillingness of the board to take any chances whatsoever. You should relax your program so as to permit a farmer to borrow money to clear land, to clear off scrub, and so on. The attitude should be a little more generous. The government of Canada can afford to take a little loss on a tremendously useful program such as this.
Another thing I hear from many people is that they will not accept the loans because they have to sign so many papers. They have to give their age and the age of their wives, when they were married', and all about this, that and the other thing. They have to give

their fingerprints. So many papers have to be filled out that they feel it is not worthwhile, so the loans are limited to very good risks, to people who are very objective, and so on. This thing is fine; it is helping the banks out, and in some places it is taking the place of banks, but it should be widened a bit to take in the newer areas where people are taking chances every day. They should really have the benefit of this fine financial set-up.

Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this resolution relating to the salary of the chief electoral officer. I wish at the outset to say that the present incumbent of the office, like his father before him whom most of us knew, enjoys the fullest confidence of all members of the house. I

am sure nothing we might say regarding his salary will be regarded by anyone as detracting in any way from what I have just said. Indeed, there is no question that, in the light of his responsibilities and the way he discharges them, any proposal for a reasonable increase in his salary would meet with the approval of members of the house.
However I am somewhat surprised at the way in which this resolution reads, particularly in view of the rather warm discussion we had in the house last year regarding the salaries of the civil service commissioners. The Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) who introduced the resolution and bill on that occasion will recall that, prior to last year, the salaries of the civil service commissioners were fixed by statute, although for a number of years they had a supplement by means of items in the estimates.
We had asked on a number of occasions, in keeping with the recommendation by the Auditor General, that that practice should be discontinued, and that the entire amount of the salaries paid to the civil service commissioners should be provided in the statute itself. To our amazement, when the amending legislation came in it took away from parliament altogether the fixing of the salaries of the civil service commissioners and placed that matter in the hands of the governor in council. We protested strongly against that course of action. I still think we were right in our contention that the salaries of the civil service commissioners should be fixed by parliament rather than by the governor in council.
We pointed out at that time that in our opinion there were certain officials who must always be recognized as officials not of the government but of parliament. We included in that category not only the civil service commissioners but the Auditor General and the chief electoral officer. Indeed in our opposition to the proposal to make the salaries of the civil service commissioners subject to decision by the governor in council we gave as examples of a better way to do it the fact that the salaries of the Auditor General and the chief electoral officer were fixed by statute.
Despite the argument we put up at that time against changing that way of doing things, and despite considerable editorial support from newspapers in respect of the stand we took, we now find the government changing the basis with respect to the salary of the chief electoral officer. As a matter of fact we have now neither one method nor the other, but rather a hybrid. It used to be that this salary, like that of the Auditor General and of the civil service commissioners, was fixed by statute. In respect of the civil

service commissioners the salaries are no longer fixed by statute, but rather by the governor in council. In the present instance we have a proposal to fix lower and upper limits, leaving it to the governor in council to determine what the salary of the chief electoral officer will be, within those limits. I am not sure whether this is better or worse than the other arrangement; but, on balance, I think it is worse.
Our concern about the whole matter is that these people, who are servants of parliament in a particular way, and not servants of the government, should not have their salaries or anything related to their work handled in such a way as to make them feel that it is the government they must regard as their employer, and that it is the government to whom they must go to obtain increases in salaries.
I deeply regret that the government has taken this course of action with respect to people in this position. I regret it because of the nature of the position itself; I regret it because of the person of the present incumbent, and I do not think this change should be made.
Another feature about the change that puzzles me is that the resolution proposes that the salary shall not be less than $8,000 or more than $12,000 per year. If my information is correct the present salary is $10,000, and I am puzzled as to why we find here this sliding scale with provision for a salary lower than that now received by the present incumbent. That being so, the chief electoral officer just does not know what can happen. He might get an increase from the government but, on the other hand, the government might decide to decrease his salary. I insist that this is not fair. In my view the chief electoral officer should continue to enjoy in all respects and in every way the status he has enjoyed across the years, as a servant of parliament rather than of the government.
I shall be interested in any explanation the Secretary of State may give for this change, either in committee or at any other stage. However, I do feel that this is the wrong way to go about it; and I regret very much that the government has paid so little heed to what we on this side of the house thought was a pretty strong and effective argument put forward last year. At that time if the measure which had been brought before the house had been changed, the prestige of the government might have been damaged. On the other hand, I remember the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) agreeing to a change when persuaded by the house that he had made a wrong move.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution changes the present law in two respects. One is to displace the fixed salary provided by the statute and to substitute a floor and ceiling, the floor being lower than the present statutory salary and the ceiling being higher. The other change is to remove from parliament the responsibility for establishing the salary and to vest that responsibility and power in the governor in council.
I do not think anyone in this house is going to argue that parliament should set the salary of every public official, but there certainly are some outstanding oases where parliament and not the governor in council should set the salary. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, that applies eminently to the Auditor General. He is an official of parliament, and parliament should establish his salary. There should be no power left in the governor

Canada Elections Act
in council in respect of the amount of salary to be received by an official like the Auditor General who must enjoy complete independence of the government.
The same thing can be said about the official whose salary is under debate at this moment, namely the chief electoral officer. Independence in the administration of the duties of his office is just as important in my submission as independence in the administration of the duties of the Auditor General. Why this office should be singled out now as one in which the governor in council should claim the right to fix the salary is something I cannot follow.
This resolution does not propose to create a new office. We are not dealing with a situation where there has been no history. Here we have an official whose independence of the government has been guaranteed by the fact that his salary is fixed by parliament in a statute. The government can take nothing from him. Why change? That is the big question: Why should a change be made now? It would be quite possible within the limits proposed in the present resolution for the governor in council to apply pressure upon the salary hopes of *the official holding this high office.
It seems to me entirely unsound to propose that any measure be adopted which will qualify or modify in any degree the independence of the chief electoral officer. Let us compare this proposal with what was involved ini the resolution which has just been disposed of by the house. In that case the house decided that the present provisions of the Tariff Board Act by which the salaries of the vice-chairman and the third member of the board are fixed shall continue. No member of this house I am sure is going to suggest that the independence of the chief electoral officer is one whit less important than the independence of the vice-chairman and the third member of the tariff board.
I submit that what is involved here is inherently wrong. If the government is convinced that there should be an increase in the salary of the chief electoral officer I am sure the house will be glad to consider such a proposal on its merits, and consider it sympathetically, but to make an occasion of that kind the pretext for removing from parliament the right to guarantee the independence of the chief electoral officer from all government influence seems to me to be a very different matter, and a move which the government ought not to make.
It seems to me also this measure uses what may be considered the occasion of a proper increase in the salary of the chief electoral

officer as an excuse or pretext for establishing, in lieu of parliamentary authority, governmental authority to establish that salary. That would be a retrograde step. I hope the government will withdraw this resolution. If there is occasion for increasing the salary of the chief electoral officer let us proceed to do it by a proper amendment to the act, not by this move which I submit is inherently wrong and unsound.
