After looking into the situation I decided to recommend that the duty of 5 per cent be suspended for one year. Then we will see. If at that time the imports are mainly from the United Kingdom, the suspended rate may be reimposed. I think that matter was satisfactorily taken care of.
Then there were some representations that the lowering of duty on window glass would be injurious to domestic manufacturers; but after considering these representations I arrived at the conclusions that the injury was more imaginary than real.
In the plastics field we have had some representations that the reductions in certain categories of duties would prove embarrassing to the manufacturers of certain types of plastics. However, after considering the report of the tariff board with the chairman of the board, the commissioner of tariffs and others, I have come to the conclusion that those fears are probably unfounded. In any case we shall continue to watch the situation. This is an extremely complicated field. The tariff board made an exhaustive investigation extending over some time, as the committee is aware. I would be reluctant at this time to vary the findings of the board. We shall see how it works out over the next year or two. If it is found that further changes are needed, they can be introduced.
I think those are the main representations, speaking generally. I have had no other serious representations as to the proposed tariff changes.

Mr. Chairman, I know that all members of the committee have a great deal of confidence in the chairman of the tariff board. I do not think there is a more responsible or more devoted public servant anywhere than Mr. Hector McKinnon. I am wondering what the position will be in the light of what the minister has just now said about re-examining the situation in the light of the effects of the proposed changes in the tariff. Will there be any complications in the way of restoring the present provisions, or in other words of neutralizing the proposed changes? For instance, will there be any complications as a result of our international agreements if it should be found that the effects of the changes now proposed are not as happy as the minister indicates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We shall watch the situation fairly closely. The principal complaint I have received about the plastics schedule is as the result of an import reduction in the type of plastics known as phenol plastics for making laminated board, bakelite and that sort of thing. I have concluded, as I say, that those fears are not too well founded, but we shall

Customs Tariff
have to see. This recommendation represents the considered view of the tariff board. As the committee knows, the board has recommended some reductions and some increases, and the reason is that this is a very complex field. Technical processes have been changing over the last ten or fifteen years since the tariff schedules were written with respect to it.
I do not know whether any hon. members have seen the editorial in the most recent issue of the magazine Canadian Plastics. I do not want to take the time of the committee to read the whole of the editorial, but perhaps I shall read one paragraph from it. It says:
We have had a chance to read the copy of the report of the tariff hoard re the plastics industry, and in the opinion of your editor, it is perhaps one of the most credible documents ever compiled on any industry, by any board, at any time.
I shall leave out the next paragraph which refers to the members of the board, and then the article continues:
It is impossible for any board on tariff matters to recommend a course which will not cause a "backbite" from certain individuals who might be adversely affected. Undoubtedly, this report will have its hecklers.
Albeit . . . but when the report is read, digested, analyzed and finally comprehended in its full intent . . . there will be few ... if any at all . . . who will refute the fact that the board was interested only in fostering the most healthy national development of the plastics industry in all its phases.
That is in general terms, but it does give some indication of the appreciation of the report and recommendations which have been made by the board.

Would the minister deal with the other point I raised, as to the possibility of our hands being tied by our present international agreements should it be found that the effects of the present changes are not as expected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not fully appreciate the import of the hon. member's question. We can go back to where we were before the introduction of this measure. Nothing we do in this measure will tie our hands so far as reverting to our former position is concerned. I think that answers what the hon. member had in mind.

Will the minister say a word about the situation which exists as between the United States administrative officials, who are actually carrying out the tariff measures, and those in charge of government policy? We have been told from time to time that it is very difficult to get the administrative people to carry out the intention indicated by the government. We are often told that, by delays running into weeks or even months, they impose what is

in effect something much more effective than a tariff. Can the minister indicate the situation in that regard?
While I am on my feet I should like to ask him to deal with this in his answer. There are a good many indications that United States business is becoming more tariff-minded than it has been for years. For a good many years, at any rate, we have been happily freer than we were before from tariff considerations, but I understand there is now evidence of a considerable return on the part of business to the authorities who have these matters in hand, asking for tariff assistance. Perhaps the minister would deal with this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the first point, I assume the hon. member is referring to the United States customs administrative practice, and not to our own. I have never heard any serious-
I am sorry I did not make it clear. I referred to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Over the years there has been a good deal of difficulty arising out of what might be described as the rather rigid restrictive administrative practice under the United States customs legislation. For some time there has been before congress a customs simplification bill which, I am told, is making good headway. There is a better than reasonable prospect that it will be adopted in the very near future. When it is we have reason to believe that this practice, which the hon. member has indicated amounts to almost a concealed discretionary tariff, will be improved.
As to the other question, the committee may have seen that on one or two recent occasions when making speeches in the United States-although the member for Eglinton does not like me to do it-
It's all right at the right time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-when making speeches in the United States to groups of businessmen there I have expressed some apprehension about what I conceived to be a certain resurgence of protectionist sentiment in the United States. I do not believe for a moment that it represents the majority opinion in the United States, but such things as the rider that was attached to the defence bill putting a quantitative restriction on cheese imports, the increasing number of applications to the tariff board for increases in tariffs and that sort of thing, indicate that the protectionist sections of the United States are once again attempting to get increases in tariffs. I do not believe they

will succeed. I took occasion, under the circumstances to which I have referred, both in Washington and the mid-west, to issue a friendly warning against what I believed would be the unfortunate consequences if such a policy were followed. Further than that I do not think I should go at the moment.
What is the situation in regard to cheese?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a measure before the United States congress, sponsored by the administration of course, to repeal that provision. There is a reasonable chance that it will be successful.

May I suggest to the committee that the lower the tariff imposed upon glass and these similar products, the better it will be for the people of Canada. The poultry industry is a great user of glass, and out in the west glass is very essential in home building. The use of these newer windows, the idea of letting the sunlight into the homes, calls for more and more glass. I suggest that the minister consider lowering the tariff on glass to the very lowest limit so the people of Canada can get large supplies from those people who can produce glass very cheaply. It means a great deal to the health of Canada, and I shall point out to the minister also that in the time of Henry VIII there was a tax on window panes-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Did he live in a glass house?

If I did I would not throw rocks, like the hon. member. There was a tax on window panes, and we smile at that and think it is ridiculous; yet in 1952 our friend is seriously advocating the idea of putting a huge tax on any glass window that goes into a house in western Canada.

I should like to ask the minister or the Minister of National Revenue what the up to the minute news is on dumping. I know the Minister of National Revenue made a statement a short time ago, and it read all right in Hansard but I do not think it convinced the boys back home. I ask the minister if he feels he is on top of some of the devious means which are used by means of intermediary companies, and by means of, shall we say, rather fictitious sales or not typical sales in the United States, to get goods in here at an entirely unrealistic rate and thereby create a situation which is very hard on our own businessmen?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe I made a statement earlier in the house which
Customs Tariff
still holds good. So far as the investigations which have been made by the Department of National Revenue are concerned, there is no dumping in this country within the meaning of the act. If goods are sold in -the country of origin at a fair market value and they come into this country, then that is the invoice on which customs duty and sales tax are charged.
Prior to the war we had in the Department of National Revenue investigators or appraisers who made it a point to look into the imports which came into this country from foreign countries, and they were able to give us a fair appraisal of what was the fair market value in the country of export. Recently in the department, as far as one commodity is concerned, textiles, we have had the services of an up-to-date appraiser in that particular line of goods, and we have made arrangements for the appointment of four or five others, who will give appraisals of the cost of the goods in the country of export.
I do not feel that more needs to be said at this time. Perhaps that answers the hon. member's question as to what constitutes dumping.

I do not want the minister to think I am being critical, because I know this is a very difficult job; but when he says there is no dumping I think he is a little optimistic, though of course he goes on and says no dumping within the meaning of the act. I know the sense in which he says that, but again let me say that there are a lot of people who find that what is actually going on is unsatisfactory; and it is unsatisfactory for one of two reasons: Either they are able by legal devices to legally get around the act, which there is considerable reason to believe is happening in certain cases; or it may be that the minister's investigations as to fair prices in foreign countries, however well intentioned and however sincerely made, are not adequate.
I should like to have a little more information as to just how these investigations are made. For example, I am told that a company in the United States that wishes to get rid of a surplus product will adopt ingenious methods of making sales, genuine enough sales, at prices which are artificially lower, for a certain area in the United States, an area broad enough, so it is suggested to me, to satisfy an investigation made by our department. Therefore the argument is that company A, a large company which wants to dump its products, will sell in a certain area in the United States at a lower price. They will then provide evidence whereby they will

Customs Tariff
satisfy the minister's agents that the price which is being quoted in that area is a fair price; but in fact, if you look at the essence of the transaction, as represented to me, it is not a fair price, because they are selling at an artificially low price in a comparatively small area in order to establish a low price.
Will the minister say a little more as to the method of investigation? How many sales does it need to establish a price? How widespread do these sales have to be? Would two sales in one American state, for example, establish a price; because I understand these special prices are quoted in fairly large areas, let us say a whole state. Perhaps a large state will be treated in that way. Will the minister say something on that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
As far as the investigations made by our auditors in exporting countries are concerned, I might say that they are very thorough, considering the staff we have; and we have had no objections on the part of manufacturers or exporters to Canada, particularly in the United States, to giving us all the information which we require. That inquiry is made over the territory in which the particular line of trade is carried on. For instance, if it is in the textile industry, the hon. gentleman probably knows that the chief points at which textiles are made in the United States are upon the eastern seaboard and down in the northern central states; at least, that is where most of the exports come to Canada from.
The investigation is widespread in all the mills in those particular districts. We do not take as the price at which these goods are invoiced the price for any one particular sale. We take it over a series of sales over a certain period of time. That period may not be specific, but it is over a length of time. For instance, in the textile industry there are certain things that affect it. For instance, there are climatic conditions, differences in style and all that. Manufacturers of women's summer dresses in the United States probably have them ready for the trade by January 1 for people who can afford to buy them and want to go to Florida or California. They sell those dresses to their own trade perhaps two or three months later. Naturally they can be bought earlier. These same styles, as the hon. member for Hamilton West would know, across the line are probably in vogue in Canada somewhat later on in the season. All these things have to be taken into consideration in the establishment of what is known as a fair market value; and a fair market value is a value at which these goods are sold in the country of origin under comparable conditions and to the same type of people in the trade.

What I mean is, you get the retail price and you get the jobber's price, and you get the manufacturer's price. If a jobber in the United States is selling to a jobber in Canada, then it would be the jobber's price that would govern. If somebody goes over there and brings back half a dozen dresses, then it is the retail price that governs the invoice. I want to repeat that after thorough investigation of the invoices of different types of commodities that come into this country we have not been able to find evidence of dumping.
Just recently an order was passed having to do with what is known as fixing the value. That has to do with furs, particularly muskrat and rabbit skins, that come into this country from Russia. We have hesitancy in fixing the values of that country because we do not do an awful lot of trade with them and they are not members of the GATT. Under that agreement it is the most-favourednation tariff that works, and a country like Russia would come under the general tariff.
I do not know that there is any further explanation I can give, except to restate that we have augmented our appraisers, and in the department we engage the services of people who are expert in the particular line of business. For instance, the people who put valuations on textiles are textile-trained people.
They were not a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I am talking about now.
You had a hardware merchant on that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Probably it is the government of from 1930 to 1935 that the hon. member has reference to.
No, it was not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That does not obtain at the present time.
It did in 1940.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Our textile appraisers are versed in the textile business. The people who make the appraisals on machinery that comes in here know the machine business, and so on along the line; so we are in a position, with the experience of these people and with the information we get now from the exporters in the country of origin, to determine what are fair market values for imports.
As I said in the remarks I made in the budget debate last year, there were attempts at dumping into the country; but by raising the invoice price and collecting the tariff on that, and the sales tax on top of that, we

took in over $1,500,000 in tariff alone on goods that were shipped into Canada in which there was an attempt to dump. But dumping into Canada has not been carried out successfully.

The minister began to say a word about the situation when we are dealing with countries behind the iron curtain, but he did not discuss the matter in detail. I should like to know more about how we arrive at prices, for example, in Czechoslovakia and other countries. How does the department arrive at a fair market value?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I will admit we have difficulty in getting information from countries behind the iron curtain. At the present time negotiations are under way between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and representatives of Czechoslovakia to see if they would admit our officers into their country to find out the costs of their manufactured articles.
When the minister says he has had difficulty does he mean he does not get the information?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is right. I said we have difficulties; but I wish my hon. friend would not try to misconstrue my words. If he would just listen-
I just asked a question. The minister need not be so touchy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I am not touchy at all. I am the least touchy of anyone here.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Laugh, if you like; it is just like water off a duck's back so far as I am concerned. But I said we were making attempts to do it and I admitted immediately that we have not been successful. But that does not deter us from continuing in our efforts to achieve the objective we would like to attain.

That being so, I submit the fair market value prevalent in Canada should be the determining factor, if we have any difficulty whatsoever in procuring evidence as to the fair market value in the country of origin.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 1 carry?
No, we have not yet had an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was an assertion, not a question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
It is spelled out in the statute. It is the fair market value in the country of origin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have had occasion to say it before, but I shall say again that Mr. Fielding introduced in 1909, 1910 or 1911 provisions in the tariff respecting dumping, and those have been the bible of Canadian manufacturers since that time. The provision is that the dumping duty shall be the difference between the fair market value in the country of origin at the time of export and the price at which it is invoiced. That is the statute. I think it would be found in the manufacturing side of the industry that there would not be too many people interested in tampering with that statute.
Would the minister say something as to the program now before the tariff board? There is a broad situation being reviewed, and I think it might be of interest if we were told about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have made one or two references to the tariff board, but offhand I do not recall just what they were. Of course the tariff board is continually occupied with its statutory responsibility of hearing appeals from importers or others who feel that the tariff is not properly interpreted, or some other question appealed to the tariff board from a decision by the Department of National Revenue.
The tariff board has cleaned up these matters. The committee will recall that in my budget I recommended a small increase in shot and grit, for the reasons there stated. I thought I should consider the matter further before acting upon it. That is shot and grit used in the manufacture of castings.
There will be less Grit after tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was wondering whether my hon. friend would wish to make one of his witticisms.

As we look at the international trade situation, would the minister state whether there is any likelihood of further trade conferences, or if we have caught our breath since the last one. What is the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no immediate prospect of any further conferences, such as those at Geneva, Torquay and Annecy. The field appears to have been pretty well exhausted for the time being. In view of the fact that this is a presidential election year in the United States, and for other reasons, I doubt whether there is any immediate prospect of any further general conferences of that kind.
As my hon. friend will recall, the agreements run until the end of 1953. Of course the whole situation will have to be examined prior to that time.

On section 1-Definitions.

speechtext: I shall try to get that information in a moment. I do not have it readily available. It will be noted that section 1 is purely a drafting amendment. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue has the revenue statistics with him and will be able to give that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The collections for succession duties in 1951, the last year for which we have statistics, were $33,599,089.

minister figures for any previous years?
[Mr. Abbott.)

Last session the Dominion Elections Act was retitled "Canada Elections Act." Why was one act treated in that way when this act is still left as "Dominion Succession Duty Act"? Can the minister tell the house what is the government's policy in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am grateful to the hon. member for calling the matter to my attention. I think it would be quite proper to change the title of this act. The general policy has been that where an act is opened up and the descriptive word is "dominion", that word is changed to "Canada". It was simply an oversight on my part that that was not done in this case. Perhaps we can take care of that next year when we are dealing with the general revision.

Further to the remarks I made during the debate on the budget, may I say that I have been very interested in what this bill might provide. I recognize the difficulties under which the minister is labouring in presenting these amendments and I appreciate also that an over-all revision of the act is imminent. Nevertheless I want to take advantage of this opportunity to urge upon the minister once more that when the major revision is under consideration he give attention to the incidence of double taxation which has occurred in the past in connection with such cases as I mentioned before. I shall not go into them again, but inasmuch as the revision of the act is under consideration and plans are being made to that end I hope this matter will be taken under consideration and not overlooked in the general revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should indicate that consideration was given to this. My parliamentary assistant told me that my hon. friend had raised this question. The present provisions of the law covering the taxation of pensions have been developed after a great deal of consideration. We have had a number of representations along the lines of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Hamilton West. They have been studied, but it is considered- that the present law is a fair and workable arrangement for handling a very complicated part of any tax system.
When a widow is in receipt of a pension she is regarded as receiving the right to income which may be valued having regard to the terms of the pension and her life expectancy. It is considered fair that such value be part of the estate for succession duty

purposes because an equivalent value of property to provide a similar income for the widow would be liable for succession duties. When the widow receives income, whether from a pension or in any other form, she is subject to income tax in the same way as any other taxpayer. However, that point will be further considered when the act is under general revision.

There is only the fact that with the application of the succession duty to the value of the pension the net income to the widow is reduced in the first instance. Then when income tax is applied on subsequent income from the estate, whether it be from a pension or from other property, there is a type of double taxation which I would urge the minister to study very carefully when the act is being amended.

May I ask the minister if in connection with the revision of the act consideration is being given to the present so-called "notch" provision, and whether the government will consider applying an exemption of $50,000 instead of simply exempting estates under $50,000. I do not think I need to enlarge any further on the subject. It has been discussed here before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am aware of the situation.
There are many complications as a result of this present provision. I shall not enlarge on it, but I do hope the matter will be given serious consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think every aspect of the act will be considered.

On section 2-Marriage consideration.
Has the minister considered whether the community property law in Quebec as between husband and wife may have any effect on this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think the community law provisions would enter into this section. This is a loophole section. We had a decision in the province of Quebec which interpreted the section of the act as it now stands in a way it was felt parliament never intended it to be. As the explanatory note points out, this amendment together with the amendment to section 8, which is carried out by section 4 of the bill, we believe will make it quite clear that property transferred or agreed to be transferred in consideration of marriage will be exempt from succession duty only if such transfers or settlements were actually executed or fulfilled more than three years before the death of the deceased.
Dominion Succession Duty Act
The general rule is that such transfers must be effected within a certain time limit if they are to escape the provisions of the act. This amendment is to make clear what it was thought had been made clear in the original act, but which the courts held had not been made clear. I do not think the community rights in the province of Quebec will be affected in any way.
What is the relative situation in the various provinces? Are there different provisions for different areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The general rule is that a conveyance, whether as a result of a marriage contract or a gift or anything else, must have been made more than three years prior to the decease in order to not be included for succession duty purposes.
Is that a general provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the general provision which applies to all transfers throughout Canada. If they are to avoid the application of death duties they must be made a certain period of time prior to the decease. Transfers within that period of time are by law deemed to be made in contemplation of death.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That may be, but so much the better for the taxpayer. He gets the benefit.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Fair market value.

Would the minister explain the effect of this section so as to indicate what the situation would be in the case of a private company, the owner of the company not having taken advantage for a period of two or three years of section 95A of the Income Tax Act, having accumulated undistributed profits in the company, and then dying? Would the effect of this amendment be to have the successor pay the succession duties on the undistributed profits, a part of which would eventually be paid over in the form of income tax by the company or by the successor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend's question, that is one of the reasons section 95A was introduced. It was realized in the case of certain private companies, where earnings had been allowed to accumulate and had not been distributed or reinvested in the business, that upon the death of the shareholder the value of the shares would include capital in the company and the accumulated profits. In order to get those profits out they would of course, when distributed as dividends, be subject to income tax. It was for that reason section 95A was enacted. This amendment is to spell out in our act, as I know it is spelled out in the Ontario act, the provision that under such circumstances no account shall be taken of a possible liability for income tax when profits are distributed. For obvious reasons I think that could not be taken into account because the amount of income tax which would be payable would depend upon the bracket in which the individual shareholder happened to be, what other income he had, and so on. Therefore there is a means now available in the law to enable people

in that position to protect themselves against excessive liability for both succession duties and income tax.
In answer to my hon. friend's question, it is and always has been the law that the fair market value must include whatever is in the assets of a company at the time of death and that no account shall be taken of any potential income tax liability.
Why was this clause necessary? Were there certain circumstances under which the income tax payable was deducted twice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was a case in one of the provinces, I believe British Columbia, where it was held that might be the result of our law as enacted at the present time. This section is putting into our law what I know is in the Ontario law.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 8 agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 207, to amend the Excise Act, 1934.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson in the chair.
On section 1-"Spirits."
Will the minister give us an expert opinion as to just what the effect of this change of wording is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not an expert in the material which is included in this section; but I think the explanatory note indicates clearly the purpose of the section. It is as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to require that the provisions of the Excise Act in respect to alcohol shall be applicable to all spirits produced whether by the ordinary process of distillation or other means.
I am informed that, as is indicated in the explanatory note, this definition has been contained in the schedule for some years and is now being merely transferred to the definition section of the act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6-Offences for sale of spirits unlawfully' manufactured, etc.

I have one question on clause 6, under subsection 3 of section 169. This 55704-164
Excise Act
is the subsection which applies to the forfeiture of vehicles in which are found spirits which are sold or offered for sale and which have not been lawfully manufactured or lawfully imported and so on. I should like to ask the minister whether any consideration is being given to some review of the provisions of the act generally in regard to the forfeiture of vehicles. I think there must be a good many cases in which the innocent owner of a vehicle has been grossly imposed upon by someone who has taken advantage of him for the purpose of obtaining transportation for goods of this kind. The same thing applies to tobacco which has been unlawfully manufactured or unlawfully imported.
The sections of the act at present are extremely severe, it seems to me, with respect to forfeiture in these cases. As long as there are such sections on the statute books I presume the officials concerned are not going to have a free hand in these matters; they are going to feel obliged to proceed with severity as long as the terms of the statute themselves are severe. I should like to ask the minister whether consideration is being given or study is being applied to the provisions of the act generally with reference to the forfeiture of vehicles. I am satisfied that there are innocent owners of vehicles who are imposed upon by people who are found to be carrying goods unlawfully imported or unlawfully manufactured.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend appreciates, this seqtion relates only to spirits which are taken from bonded premises and which are sold.
I appreciate that. My question was with respect to subsection 3 of section 169, and to forfeiture generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is probably thinking of the fellow who innocently carries in his car a few cigarettes that have been brought in from outside Canada.
When the passenger in his car has cigarettes in his bag of which the innocent owner of the car is not aware. There are cases where innocent owners of vehicles are imposed upon by their passengers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that the number of innocent victims of that kind is comparatively small and that such cases are rare; and that in any case where it is established that they are innocent, the minister takes steps by proper remission to release the car.
I am told that no consideration has been given to relaxing the provisions of the law with respect to seizures. In view of the assertions that have been made in the

Excise Act
House of Commons as to the increase in smuggling in certain products, I think it would be unwise at this time to relax the provisions of the law which provide enforcement officers with a reasonable opportunity of enforcing the law.
Perhaps you will have to find a better means of dealing with the problem.

With the consent of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I should like to revert to section 5 for a moment in order to ask the minister this question. What is the significance of the reference to the Unfair Competition Act, and what is the necessity for reserving this discretion with regard to the form and wording?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no change in this section except for the words "and the Food and Drugs Act".

I realize
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to answer that question, but I will see what information I can get from my officials. I am told the purpose of the amendment is to inform the people who are in the business of packaging and so on that there are these three acts to be considered.

While I
appreciate that it is not a change in the act, will the minister indicate what is the practical need for the reservation of a discretion in the minister as to form and wording? Does that in fact take place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told it is meant to ensure that no false and misleading statements are made on the label which is put on these products.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-Penalty.
Before we pass clause 7, Mr. Chairman, I want a chance to look at it. This is of assistance to the ordinary private citizen, apparently. Is the minister coming to his rescue and trying to-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is homebrew. The former definition did not cover the man who made beer out of extracts or other synthetic products.
Apparently if you press this wording strongly, a man cannot make beer for himself alone. It has to be for himself and his family. Would that be the interpretation of the wording?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that he can make application to the collector and get permission to make beer for his own consumption, but he must not get into the commercial field. I have never tried it myself.

Section agreed to.
Sections 8 to 12 inclusive agreed to.
Schedule agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 206, to amend the Excise Tax Act. .

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Furs.

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure to welcome a bill that makes reduction in taxes. I should like to ask the minister a question on this bill in general, with reference to the 1952 increases applied under the Excise Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I refer to the increases in rates from 15 per cent to 25 per cent. Are all those increases with respect to all commodities to which they applied now removed by this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct, they are all reduced from 25 per cent to 15 per cent.

The other part of my question is with respect to taxes which last year were introduced at the rate of 15 per cent on the commodities then designated. Is that 15 per cent tax now removed with respect to all the commodities on which it was applied by the 1951 amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I believe the minister made some comment earlier in the evening regarding Russian furs which are a menace to our northern trappers. I understand they reach the Canadian market, and I wonder if this section would not be of assistance in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was with respect to custom duties on Russian furs. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue indicated that with respect to those importations fixed valuations were being applied for customs duties purposes.
Is this 15 per cent tax on raw furs or processed furs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On processed furs.
I want to know who places the market value on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that usually the value taken is the invoice of the purchaser to the dresser and dyer, but if the officers of the Department of National Revenue have reason to believe that is not the fair value they may put an appraised value on them.

The reason I mention this is that I have an invoice which was made out just before this amendment, and it shows that a lady purchased a silver fox skin for $10. Then she sent it to the processor, but the government would not accept the valuation of $10, for which she had a receipt. The government officials valued the skin at $24, and the 25 per cent tax was then imposed upon that valuation. I have always argued that the government had no right to put a tax on the raw skin, but that is overcome by saying that the skin is going to be processed and when it is processed it is not a raw skin. This lady was charged $6 on this skin. When the article was made up she had paid the government $14.40 in taxes, which was nothing less than pure robbery.
I used a stronger word the other day and the minister took me up on it by letter. I used the word "gyp" so this time I used the word "robbery", which is not so strong. Why should the government put a different valuation on the skin which is sent in to be processed when a person has an invoice for $10. They charged her the tax on their valuation of $24, and I want to know whether or not an invoice should be accepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It usually is. The law requires that the tax be imposed on the current market value. If the invoice is for less than the current market value, then the skin has to be appraised at what is, in fact, the current market value.

I think there should be some definition of "market value". If it is going to be the market value, then why should it not be the price which this lady paid for the skin? I do not think the government or any of its officials should say that it should have been a higher price. When the lady received the article for which she had paid $10, she found that she had to pay the government $14.40, so she said she would not take it. If the government had taxed her on the $10, as they should have, then it would have made quite a difference.

While we are on that subject, will the minister state by what criterion the government does determine the market value?
55704-164J
Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is set out in the law, and I shall be glad to inform the hon. member of it. The regulation reads:
The "current market value of furs" referred to in subsection 1 of section 80A of The Excise Tax Act, means in addition to the cost of the raw furs to the owner, all costs of freight, cartage, exchange in effect on the date of shipment, insurance, royalties and duty for delivering the furs to him, and in addition, the charges for dressing and dyeing.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Repeal.
This is the section, I believe, which covers automobiles, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

I should like to speak about the situation which arose with the reduction of the tax, as related to automobiles which were in the hands of dealers under consignment contracts, upon which the department insisted on collecting the tax despite the fact that a legal contract had been drawn and the cars had been shipped by the manufacturer and were on the premises of the dealers. I understand that the department's attitude was that the goods having moved out of the manufacturer's warehouse and into the premises of dealers, that constituted delivery. I should like to draw attention to the fact that at this time the dealers were well stocked up with cars, and on the other hand the manufacturers had more cars on hand than they had space in the warehouses. This situation was the subject of considerable discussion between the manufacturers and the dealers.
With a budget imminent and the knowledge that it was quite likely something would be done about the tax, the dealers were very reluctant to take delivery of automobiles. In an effort to relieve the congestion at the manufacturers' warehouses these contracts were drawn, and in good faith the dealers took delivery of cars which they placed in warehouses. This contract was not recognized by the government, and I submit that it was wrong to assess the dealers a tax on property which they had not legally acquired. The contract had been drawn up and legally executed, so it should have been acknowledged by this government. I submit that it is wrong, and that these dealers have been subjected to a hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter is one of some concern. It is a question of law, and was brought to the attention of the Department of Justice. One company in particular, General Motors, did this consignment. The Department of Justice gave the following

Excise Tax Act
opinion, and this is the deputy minister of justice speaking:
I am of opinion that the agreement entered into between General Motors and its dealers is an agreement to sell and, consequently, the dealers are purchasers under the agreement.
Excise and sales taxes under sections 80 and 86 of the Excise Tax Act are payable at the time of delivery of the goods to the purchaser and I am of opinion, therefore, that the taxes are payable in this case when the goods are delivered by General Motors to its dealers.
In the light of that opinion the Department of National Revenue had no option but to collect the tax. The other companies evidently had some doubt as to the legality of the procedure and did not adopt it.
I appreciate the position the dealers were in, and I indicated to one who came to see me the other day that if in their opinion the Department of Justice were wrong, then they should lodge an appeal. We would facilitate a test case, and if the opinion of the Department of Justice were overruled, and it was held that no tax was legal, we would be very happy to make refunds. Whether or not that is going to be done I do not know.

The difficulty is that by the time the dealer takes his case to court
he will probably spend as much in legal fees as he would save in tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think General Motors ought to look after the case for him.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
